items.title: Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye et moi : Itiniraire d’une personnalité atypique (
items.description: De la réussite des JOJ Dakar 2026 au legs d'une génération lumineuse… ! Il est des parcours qui ne se racontent pas uniquement à travers les fonctions exercées, les titres obtenus ou les responsabilités assumées. Ils se comprennent aussi à travers les époques qu'ils traversent, les rencontres qu'ils suscitent, les convictions qu'ils portent et les empreintes qu'ils laissent dans la mémoire collective. Le parcours de Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye appartient à cette catégorie de trajectoires singulières. Avec Dakar 2026, le Sénégal n'a pas simplement accueilli une compétition sportive internationale. Il a franchi un seuil symbolique dans son histoire et dans celle du continent africain. Pour la première fois, les Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse se sont installés sur une terre africaine, donnant à une nouvelle génération l'occasion de rencontrer le monde sur son propre continent. Derrière cette ambition, il y a eu des institutions, des engagements politiques, des moyens financiers, des femmes et des hommes. Il y a également eu un parcours personnel, celui d'un dirigeant qui aura consacré une part importante de sa vie au mouvement sportif et à son rayonnement international. C'est cette histoire que je souhaite brièvement raconter afin que nul n’en ignore car c’est aussi celle d’une amitié personnelle, fraternelle indéfectible, forte affectueuse et fusionnelle renforcée par les bons présages et prières de nos parents. Une exceptionnelle aventure humaine que rien ne pourra altérer… Celle d’une jeunesse résolue à arpenter le monde avec ambition, courage, pugnacité avec comme valeurs essentielles et force majeure, notre bonne éducation et instruction, nos talents, notre courage ainsi que nos idées et idéaux de jeunes déterminés à jouer une partition dans un monde qui subissait le choc de la fin des « 30 glorieuses » période faste de l’après seconde guerre mondiale (1945 – 1975). Comment un homme, au croisement du monde économique, du sport et des relations internationales, a-t-il contribué à inscrire le Sénégal dans une nouvelle séquence de l'histoire mondiale de l’Olympisme ? Ce que l'histoire retient, ce que le temps révèle, ce que les générations transmettent… Il arrive, au terme d'un parcours, que l'on éprouve le besoin de s'arrêter, de prendre du recul et de regarder le chemin parcouru. Non pour dresser un inventaire de distinctions, de responsabilités ou de réalisations, mais pour tenter de comprendre ce qui, au-delà des événements, demeure véritablement attaché à une personnalité. Le parcours de Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye invite à cet exercice. Banquier d’affaires reconnu, positionné aux confluents et affluents de la finance internationale, dirigeant sportif, acteur du mouvement olympique international et figure centrale de l'aventure olympique sénégalaise, il aura traversé plusieurs univers, parfois éloignés les uns des autres, mais reliés par un même fil conducteur : celui de l'engagement, des relations humaines, de la confection de liens stratégiques et de la recherche d'une place pour le Sénégal dans les grandes dynamiques internationales. Son itinéraire n'est pas celui d'une trajectoire linéaire. Il est fait de rencontres, d'opportunités, de convictions, de responsabilités et de paris sur l'avenir. Il témoigne aussi d'une époque où les frontières entre économie, sport, diplomatie et influence internationale sont devenues de plus en plus poreuses. Dakar 2026 : bien plus que des Jeux L'organisation des Jeux Olympiques de la Jeunesse à Dakar constitue incontestablement un moment majeur de cette histoire. Pour la première fois, le continent africain a accueilli un événement olympique. Cette première n'est pas seulement une consécration sportive. Elle représente une reconnaissance symbolique, une ouverture diplomatique et une invitation faite à l'Afrique de prendre toute sa place dans l'univers des grandes manifestations internationales. Derrière les infrastructures, les cérémonies, les compétitions et la mobilisation populaire, il y a eu une ambition collective. Celle d'un pays qui a accepté de relever un défi dont la portée dépassait largement ses frontières. Dans cette aventure, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye aura occupé une place particulière. Son engagement dans le mouvement olympique, ses relations institutionnelles et son implication dans le projet des JOJ auront contribué à inscrire cette ambition dans la durée. Mais l'histoire ne saurait être celle d'un seul homme. Elle appartient également aux autorités publiques, aux équipes d'organisation, aux partenaires, aux sportifs, aux bénévoles et à toutes celles et ceux qui ont rendu cette aventure possible. C'est précisément dans cette articulation entre l'engagement individuel et la réussite collective que réside l'intérêt historique de Dakar 2026. L'œuvre au-delà de l'homme Une distinction, aussi prestigieuse soit-elle, récompense un parcours. Une responsabilité institutionnelle confère une place. Une réalisation d'envergure inscrit un nom dans la mémoire d'une époque. Cependant, le véritable héritage se mesure autrement. Il se mesure à la capacité des institutions à poursuivre leur mission, à la pérennité des infrastructures, à la transmission des compétences, à l'émergence de nouveaux talents et à la faculté d'une génération de transformer une expérience exceptionnelle en acquis durables. C'est ici que se situe l'un des grands enjeux de l'après-Dakar 2026. Le Village olympique, les équipements sportifs, les infrastructures d'accueil, les compétences acquises dans l'organisation de grands événements et les réseaux internationaux mobilisés devront trouver une nouvelle vocation au service du développement national. La réussite d'un événement ne devient un héritage que lorsqu'elle continue de produire des effets après que les projecteurs se sont éteints. Le legs d'une génération lumineuse Au-delà de la personnalité de Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, cette contribution aura également voulu raconter une génération. Une génération d'hommes et de femmes qui, à différentes échelles, ont investi leurs compétences, leurs relations, leur énergie et parfois leur audace dans la construction d'une ambition nationale et africaine. Une génération qui a connu les limites des possibles, mais qui a aussi appris à les repousser. Une génération qui a compris que le rayonnement international d'un pays ne repose pas uniquement sur ses ressources naturelles, sa puissance économique ou son poids diplomatique, mais également sur sa capacité à porter des projets, à fédérer des énergies et à inspirer confiance. Dakar 2026 aura donné un visage à cette ambition. La question qui se pose désormais est celle de la transmission. Comment faire en sorte que les jeunes Sénégalais et Africains ne soient pas simplement les spectateurs d'une réussite passée, mais les acteurs des transformations à venir ? Comment transmettre les expériences, les méthodes, les réseaux et les enseignements de cette aventure à ceux qui auront demain la responsabilité de poursuivre l'œuvre ? Car une génération ne laisse véritablement son empreinte que lorsqu'elle prépare celle qui luI succède. L'homme face au jugement du temps Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye appartient désormais à une histoire qui mérite d'être documentée, interrogée et transmise. Son parcours, comme toute trajectoire humaine et institutionnelle, doit pouvoir être regardé dans sa complexité : ses réussites, ses choix, ses engagements, ses convictions, mais également les interrogations et les débats que suscitent les grandes responsabilités. L'ambition de cette contribution n'aura donc pas été de construire une légende, encore moins de figer un homme dans une image définitive. Elle aura été de restituer un itinéraire, d'en comprendre les ressorts, d'en mesurer la portée et d'en interroger les prolongements. Car les hommes passent, les fonctions changent, les circonstances évoluent. Les œuvres, elles, ne survivent que lorsqu'elles sont entretenues, prolongées et enrichies par d'autres. Et c'est peut-être là que se trouve la véritable mesure d'un parcours : non pas seulement dans ce qu'un homme aura accompli de son vivant, mais dans ce que les générations suivantes pourront encore construire à partir de son expérience. Son mot de clôture des JOJ de DAKAR 2026 en dit long : « Les Jeux auront leur histoire, les médailles leurs palmarès, les distinctions leurs archives. Mais le véritable héritage de Dakar 2026 se mesurera à ce que la jeunesse africaine osera entreprendre demain. » MDN L'homme, l'œuvre et le temps. Une trajectoire individuelle. Une ambition collective. Un héritage à transmettre. L'histoire retiendra peut-être Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye comme l'une des figures qui auront accompagné l'entrée de l'Afrique dans une nouvelle dimension de l'histoire olympique. Mais le jugement le plus important appartiendra au temps : celui qui dira si l'élan de Dakar 2026 aura véritablement contribué à ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives aux générations africaines. Car au fond, la grandeur d'une œuvre ne réside pas seulement dans le moment où elle s'accomplit, mais dans la lumière qu'elle continue de projeter sur l'avenir. Ousman Blondin DIOP Ancien Ministre Conseiller, Délégué Permanent du Sénégal auprès de l’UNESCO

items.title: French Ambassador to Ghana warns of AI threats, urges Africa not to ‘wait for the West’
items.description: French Ambassador to Ghana, Diarra Dimé-Labille, has sounded an alarm over the potential threats of Artificial Intelligence, warning that humanity could be approaching a crossroads where its ability to control the technology and determine its own destiny could increasingly come into question. She believes the dangers are too significant to ignore, insisting that Ghana and the African continent must lead the charge in shaping the future of AI and establishing safeguards to protect humanity. The Ambassador says the continent must not wait for global technology giants in the West to determine how a technology, whose consequences will affect every society, operates. Speaking during a diplomatic visit to the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), she expressed concern about how quickly AI is evolving and whether humanity is adequately prepared to manage its potential risks. “Ghana and the African countries, the European countries, and all those countries can do something together. We are responsible. There is no need to wait for others to do it for us. And it’s not only the expert or the scientific that has to deal with it. It’s also all of us as citizens,” she said. The French Ambassador to Ghana and a delegation from the embassy paid a diplomatic visit to KNUST to acquaint them with the activities of the university in promoting AI education and deployment. The visit is part of a two-day tour by the ambassador to the region to inspect projects and other infrastructure being rolled out and funded by the embassy to foster socioeconomic and technological advancements. After touring the Responsible AI Lab (RAIL) at the university, the ambassador expressed hope that AI experts in the College of Engineering were also particularly concerned about the threats of the technology despite harnessing its benefits. “It’s important for us to treat this carefully. I was definitely impressed and amazed visiting the AI lab in KNUST, and one of the first reflections when I saw all those young AI experts, they were talking about safeguard. They were talking about the need for humanity to really do the best possible to contain the threat of AI,” she said. She continued: “You are an AI expert, are you not afraid? And, they told me, it’s not because we failed to prevent this kind of threat yesterday that we cannot do it today. It’s never late. “So, seeing those young Ghanaian AI experts thinking about it, having this kind of hope, makes me, very hopeful. Those young people are definitely very committed to working in a very ethical and responsible AI.” The ambassador also participated in the opening session of the Winter School at KNUST, where she reiterated France’s commitment to strengthening scientific research, academic cooperation and innovation partnerships with African countries, particularly Ghana. Ambassador Dimé-Labille highlighted that France considers Africa an important partner in scientific advancement and is keenly concerned about developing sustainable partnerships that would foster bilateral cooperation and provide practical solutions to pressing societal challenges. Meeting with some faculty members and the governing council of the university, Ambassador Dimé-Labille emphasized deepening the cooperation between the university and the embassy. “The cooperation between the French embassy and KNUST definitely needs to continue in this way. We know that we are having this cooperation and the partnership through different initiatives,” she said. Representing the Vice Chancellor, Prof Samuel Asare Nkansah, who is a professorial member of the university council, highlighted some initiatives undertaken by the university to enhance AI education and its application. He noted that the university is ready to explore AI applications in the Sustainable Development Goals, particularly ensuring social inclusion with a focus on physical challenges.

items.title: Maxwell Kudekor appointed World International Press Club International Affairs Secretary
items.description: JoyNews journalist Maxwell Kudekor has been appointed International Affairs Secretary of the World International Press Club (WIPC), an international media organisation committed to promoting press freedom, journalists’ rights and professional cooperation. The appointment was announced in a congratulatory message issued by the organisation’s International President, Ayrongozeb Kamal, who described Mr Kudekor’s appointment as a reflection of its confidence in his leadership, dedication and commitment to global journalism. The organisation expressed optimism that his experience and contributions would strengthen its international activities and promote solidarity among journalists across different countries. Press Freedom In its congratulatory message, the WIPC said it expected the newly appointed International Affairs Secretary to contribute towards strengthening international cooperation and advancing the organisation’s objectives. “We firmly believe that his experience, cooperation, and valuable contributions will help strengthen WIPC’s international activities and promote unity, solidarity, press freedom, journalists’ rights, and professional development worldwide,” the statement said. The organisation also expressed hope that the appointment would create new opportunities for international cooperation among media practitioners, wishing Mr Kudekor success in his new responsibilities and reaffirmed its commitment to promoting unity and solidarity within the journalism profession. Commitment Reacting to the appointment, Mr Kudekor reaffirmed his commitment to defending the rights of journalists and promoting responsible journalism. “Always ready to continue in the service of humanity. Defending the rights of journalists and responsible journalism,” he stated. The appointment places the Ghanaian journalist in an international role involving the promotion of cooperation among media professionals and the advancement of the WIPC’s stated objectives. About WIPC The World International Press Club is a Bangladesh-based international professional organisation of journalists established in 2023 to build unity among journalists worldwide while protecting their professional rights, safety, dignity and welfare. Its objectives include promoting press freedom, improving journalists’ working conditions, supporting journalists facing threats or persecution and encouraging professional development through training, conferences and international exchanges. The organisation also advocates ethical journalism, fact-checking, legal assistance for journalists and cooperation with media institutions and human rights organisations. WIPC’s constitution provides for international governing structures, national branches and regional coordination arrangements intended to facilitate cooperation among journalists across countries.

items.title: ‘I won’t disappoint you in my second term’ – Adeleke assures Osun people
items.description: By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo As the week-long activities to usher Governor Ademola Adeleke’s second term in office took off with Jumat service, the governor has vowed not to disappoint the people of the State. Represented by the Deputy Governor, Prince Kola Adewusi, at the Oja Oba Central mosque in Osogbo, the Governor recalled the struggles and battles for the sustenance of democracy in Osun State and vowed to continue to place the interest of the public at the heart of his administration. A statement issued by his spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, on Friday stated that the governor commended Osun people for their steadfastness, perseverance and persistent solidarity during the electioneering period, saying the state has become a national model, a symbol for people’s power as the foundation of democracy. “I won’t disappoint Osun people. I will deliver even more than my first term. I am hopeful our financial situation will soon improve with the expected resolution of the local government crisis. We will take good care of workers and all segments of the society,” the governor was quoted as saying. Earlier in his sermon, Sheikh Moruf Ishola described the recent Osun election as “unprecedented in many respects and a standout record for all students of democracy. According to him, the Osun election that re-elected Governor Adeleke broke all records in terms of its dynamics and colours, adding that “the August 15 polls defied all calculations because almighty Allah ran it. “That is why Mr Governor must not abandon God and the people. He must continue to govern with the fear of God, keep promises and serve only the interests of the people,” he submitted on behalf of the Chief Imam of Osogboland, Sheikh Musa Animasahun. The prayer session was attended by the Secretary to the State Government, Hon. Teslim Igbalaye; Osun Central Accord Senatorial candidate, Hon. Ganiyu Olaoluwa; members of the state executive council; special advisers; and top government functionaries. items.title: Quand les repères s’effondrent, préserver sa foi devient une résistance
items.description: Cloué chez moi ce vendredi 19 novembre en raison d’une fatigue physique, j’ai passé beaucoup de temps devant les chaînes d’information en continu. J’ai alors mesuré à quel point notre époque se nourrit de mensonges , de rumeurs et de médisances. Lorsque l’Homme perd ses repères moraux, il retombe dans la loi de la jungle : la raison s’efface, la conscience se tait et la déraison prend le dessus. Certains salissent par ambition politique, d’autres détournent le regard par intérêt professionnel, tandis que d’autres encore trahissent pour quelques avantages financiers. Quand la vérité devient secondaire La vérité devient secondaire dès lors que les intérêts personnels ou partisans l’emportent. La morale se marchande, la loyauté se monnaye et la dignité s’égare. Dans ces temps de confusion, préserver sa foi, sa conscience et ses valeurs représente parfois le plus difficile des combats. Car lorsque la discorde s’installe, que le mensonge devient une arme et que les repères s’effondrent, savoir prendre du recul et demeurer fidèle à ses principes constitue déjà une forme de résistance. Le Prophète Muhammad (Psl) nous a d’ailleurs enseigné cette ligne de conduite face aux périodes de troubles : « * Lorsque tu verras les gens rompre leurs engagements et perdre leur loyauté […], reste chez toi, maîtrise ta langue, attache-toi à ce que tu sais être bon, délaisse ce que tu réprouves, occupe-toi de tes propres affaires et détourne-toi de celles de la foule * » (Sunan Abi Dawud). *Azzedine Gaci est recteur de la mosquée de Villeurbanne L’article Quand les repères s’effondrent, préserver sa foi devient une résistance est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: UNICEF, Lagos raise alarm over threats to children’s rights
items.description: …As children demand free education, protection, greater say in policies By Chioma Obinna The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the Lagos State Government have called for stronger protection of children’s rights, warning that their welfare and fundamental rights are increasingly under threat and require concrete government action. The call was made on Friday during the commemoration of the 2026 World Children’s Day at the UNICEF Lagos Office, with the theme, “My Day. My Rights. My Future.” UNICEF Chief of Field Office, Lagos, Celine Lafoucriere, said children’s rights were facing growing threats globally, stressing the need for governments and other stakeholders to guarantee every child access to education, healthcare, good nutrition, clean water, sanitation and social protection. “Children’s rights are under pressure, they’re under threat, they’re being increasingly threatened throughout the world,” she said. Lafoucriere said UNICEF was working closely with the Lagos State Government to ensure that children’s rights were respected and accessible to all, particularly the most vulnerable. She emphasised the importance of social protection programmes, noting that the existence of rights did not automatically translate into access to basic necessities. “Having a right is one thing, but it’s not going to put food on the table,” she said, explaining that social protection interventions could help vulnerable children access education, healthcare and adequate nutrition. She added that Nigeria’s future depended largely on the attention and investment devoted to children today. “The child is the future, and the future of Nigeria is today,” Lafoucriere declared. The Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, Mobolaji Ogunlende, said the government remained committed to promoting the welfare, protection and development of every child but acknowledged that it could not achieve the objective without the support of other stakeholders. He urged parents, schools, communities, development partners and other stakeholders to work together to create an environment where every child felt safe, valued and heard. “We must translate what we hear today into meaningful action and commitment,” he said. Ogunlende assured the children that their contributions and concerns raised during the celebration would not end with the event but would inform government policies and practical interventions. Also speaking, the Speaker of the Lagos State Children’s Parliament, Abdulsalam Anjola, called for greater involvement of children in decisions affecting their lives, insisting that their voices must be considered in the formulation of policies concerning them. He said children were better positioned to communicate their experiences, particularly in cases involving abuse and other challenges. Anjola also urged the government to increase investment in education and provide opportunities for out-of-school children. “Education is the weapon that can instigate war,” he said, while calling for effective implementation of education policies to guarantee children access to opportunities to realise their potential. He expressed optimism that investing in children would contribute to a safer Lagos, a better Nigeria and stronger communities. A 14-year-old student of Ikeja Senior High School, Ishola Moyinoluwa, also called for greater protection of children’s rights, particularly access to basic and free education. She said every child deserved the opportunity to be heard, educated and equipped for the future. Moyinoluwa, whose artwork depicted a young boy dreaming of becoming an astronaut, said children’s aspirations could become reality through parental guidance and government support. She urged parents to provide educational, moral and social guidance for their children, while calling on the government to establish platforms where young people could express their views on issues affecting their rights and future. As part of the celebration, 80 children, divided into eight groups, participated in an art project titled, “80 Children, One Future,” through which they presented their visions of the Nigeria they hoped to see. UNICEF urged adults to listen to children’s concerns and make practical commitments to address the challenges affecting them. The Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Youth and Social Development, Pharm. Toyin Oke-Osanyintolu, also encouraged children to speak out whenever their rights were threatened. She urged them to believe in their dreams, declaring, “If you can dream it, you can do it.” Oke-Osanyintolu commended UNICEF for its continued partnership with the Lagos State Government in advancing the welfare and development of children. items.title: Mahama vows to protect Oti Region from illegal mining amid iron ore and nickel discoveries
items.description: President John Mahama says the discovery of iron ore and nickel deposits in the Oti Region presents a potential source of prosperity and job creation, but insists any decision to mine the resources must be done in a way that benefits the people of the area without destroying its serene environment. Speaking during a courtesy visit by members of the Oti Regional House of Chiefs, the President said nickel was also discovered during the search for iron ore, a mineral he described as increasingly important in the green transition because of its use in manufacturing batteries for electric vehicles. The President, however, stressed the need to protect the region’s natural environment, saying the government would not want mining activities to destroy its serene surroundings. He said, “While they were looking for iron ore, they found nickel, which has now become very important in the green transition because it’s used to make the batteries for electric vehicles. “And so, that is a potential source of prosperity and also of job creation in that area. But I want to make sure that if it is going to be mined, it is done in such a way that it will not destroy the serene environment that we have.” He said consultations would continue with traditional authorities and the youth on the discoveries. President Mahama added that if the government decides to proceed with the exploitation of the deposits, it would be done in a manner that benefits the people of the area. He also expressed satisfaction that the Oti Region had no galamsey, insisting that the government intended to maintain that status.

items.title: Mahama defends constitutional restriction on chiefs’ participation in partisan politics
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has defended the constitutional restriction barring chiefs from participating in active partisan politics, saying the provision is necessary to protect the dignity and respect of the chieftaincy institution. He said traditional rulers must remain above partisan political contests while continuing to contribute to local governance and community development. Speaking during a courtesy call by the Oti Regional House of Chiefs on Friday, November 20, 2026, the President argued that allowing chiefs to contest partisan political positions could undermine the status of the institution. “The 1992 Constitution, for very good reason, decided that chiefs should not take part in partisan politics, and it was affirmed by the Supreme Court in its interpretation of what partisan politics is,” he said. Mr Mahama questioned the appropriateness of traditional rulers competing in district assembly elections against members of their own communities. “I believe that to maintain the respect of the institution, I believe that that particular clause is appropriate because can you imagine, let’s say we’re doing district assembly elections and the whole paramount chief is standing against some small student or some butcher or some teacher or something. It doesn’t all go very well,” he said. The President, however, stressed that the restriction should not prevent chiefs from playing an active role in local governance. He said the government had maintained the constitutional provision for appointed positions on district assemblies, which provides representation for traditional authorities and other groups. Mr Mahama said the appointment criteria would ensure that chiefs, women, young people and persons with disabilities were represented in the assemblies. He urged traditional authorities to nominate representatives who would participate in assembly discussions on their behalf and report back to them on decisions taken. The President also encouraged chiefs to work closely with district chief executives and monitor how public funds allocated to district assemblies were utilised. He said traditional authorities were well placed to identify the development needs of their communities and should help guide local authorities in selecting projects that respond to those priorities.

items.title: Ooni urges FG to revive, protect textile industry
items.description: …Calls for prioritisation of Nigerian fabrics, investment in local production By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo The Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Ogunwusi, has called on the Federal Government to revive and protect Nigeria’s textile industry as part of efforts to strengthen the nation’s economic growth and development. The monarch also urged textile unions to deploy all necessary measures to safeguard the industry and encourage the patronage of locally produced fabrics. Oba Ogunwusi, represented by Olori Aderonke Adeyeye, made the call on Friday at the 38th Annual National Education Conference of the National Union of Textile, Garment and Tailoring Workers of Nigeria (NUTGTWN) and the Nigeria Textile, Garment and Tailoring Employers’ Association in Ile-Ife, Osun State. Commending the unions for organising the conference to educate their members, the monarch said an informed labour union was essential to the survival of democracy and the development of the nation. He said stakeholders must work together to restore the country’s textile industry, revive moribund mills and make locally manufactured fabrics a source of national pride. “It is important for stakeholders to protect our industry. Let us prioritise our own fabrics. Let us revive our textile mills. Let us make Made in Nigeria a badge of pride, not an apology. “We must honour labour. Every tailor, every cutter, every employer deserves dignity, fair pay and respect. Labour is not servitude; labour is nation-building. “Let us raise a new generation. Teach them craft, teach them the business, teach them discipline. Do not let this knowledge die with us,” he said. The Ooni further stressed that the survival of democracy was closely linked to economic prosperity, respect for workers and the protection of local industries. “Democracy cannot stand on empty stomachs. It cannot stand where labour is not respected. It cannot stand where industry is allowed to die. A nation that abandons its artisans abandons its future,” he added. Earlier, NUTGTWN President, Comrade Peter Godonu, urged the Federal Government to translate its commitment to industrialisation into concrete policies and investments capable of reviving the country’s struggling textile industry. Godonu said Nigeria could no longer afford to celebrate the potential of its textile sector while factories remained closed, production capacity declined and imported products continued to dominate the domestic market. He said the union would sustain its advocacy for policies that promote industrialisation, local production, decent work and the revival of the textile and garment industry. “Our Union will therefore continue to intensify its advocacy and campaign for sustainable industrialisation, local production, decent work and the revival of the textile and garment industry. “We remain available to partner with the Federal Government, state governments, employers and other stakeholders in developing and implementing practical solutions to these challenges,” he said. The NUTGTWN president noted that Nigeria possessed several advantages that could support the rebuilding of a competitive textile and garment industry. These, he said, included a large domestic market, cotton-growing potential, abundant labour, technical expertise, a vibrant fashion and garment-making industry, a youthful population and access to the wider African market through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). He, however, said political will, policy consistency, investment and strategic coordination were necessary to harness these opportunities and restore the sector to productivity. items.title: Bono Regional Minister warns MMDCEs against neglecting district security responsibilities
items.description: The Bono Regional Minister, Joseph Addae Akwaboa, has warned Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) against neglecting their security responsibilities, urging them to prioritise the effective functioning of District Security Councils (DISECs) to prevent local security threats from escalating. He said MMDCEs, as chairpersons of their respective District Security Councils, must ensure regular meetings, proper documentation of deliberations and prompt escalation of security concerns requiring regional or national intervention. Mr Akwaboa gave the directive on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at a joint workshop for the Bono, Bono East and Ahafo Regional Security Councils (REGSECs) and MMDCEs in Sunyani. The workshop, organised by the National Security Council Secretariat, was aimed at strengthening understanding and implementation of the Security and Intelligence Agencies Act, 2026 (Act 1168). Addressing participants, the Bono Regional Minister stressed that security must be treated as an integral part of local governance rather than an issue left exclusively to security agencies. He said development planning and implementation could not be separated from the security environment within which communities operate. “I wish to emphasise that security must be mainstreamed into our local governance mandate. Development, planning and implementation cannot be divorced from the security environment within which they are expected to operate,” he stated. Mr Akwaboa explained that MMDCEs occupied strategic positions in Ghana’s decentralised security architecture because of their proximity to local communities, placing them in a position to identify emerging threats and facilitate timely responses. He said District Security Councils remained important platforms for detecting warning signs, assessing local security dynamics and referring matters requiring higher-level intervention. The minister consequently called for stronger institutional relationships between Regional Security Councils and District Security Councils through regular engagement, timely communication and structured information sharing. He identified chieftaincy disputes, land conflicts, communal tensions and other localised threats as security vulnerabilities requiring continuous monitoring and proactive intervention. Mr Akwaboa said the effective implementation of Act 1168 would further strengthen the country’s security architecture by clarifying institutional mandates, operational responsibilities and accountability mechanisms. He described the legislation as a landmark in Ghana’s security sector reforms, providing a comprehensive legal framework for the organisation, coordination and oversight of national security and intelligence functions. He maintained that a common understanding of the law among regional and district authorities was necessary to avoid institutional misunderstandings and operational lapses. “A harmonised understanding of the legal framework will promote consistency in decision-making, enhance inter-agency coordination, improve information flow and minimise the possibility of administrative and operational lapses that could compromise our collective security,” he said. The minister also urged participants to uphold confidentiality, professionalism, integrity and accountability in the handling of security information. Meanwhile, the Deputy National Security Coordinator in charge of Operations, Major General Williams Azure Ayamdo (Rtd), called for improved intelligence sharing and coordinated responses to security threats across the three regions. He warned that challenges confronting the regions could escalate when early warning signs are overlooked, information is delayed, or institutional responses are fragmented. He urged REGSECs and assembly security councils to identify emerging threats, assess their implications and facilitate timely interventions before local incidents developed into wider security challenges. He also called for greater cooperation among the three regions and encouraged traditional authorities and community leaders to support efforts at identifying local tensions and promoting peaceful dispute resolution.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Plus de 90 militaires en reconversion formés aux métiers de l’agriculture et de l’élevage
items.description: Le secrétaire général du ministère de la Guerre et de la Défense patriotique, l’Intendant colonel-major Léonard Yamba Ouoba, a procédé, ce 20 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou, à la clôture d’une session de formation en agriculture et en élevage au profit de militaires en phase de reconversion. À l’issue de trois semaines d’apprentissage, plus de 90 participants ont reçu leurs attestations de participation afin de faciliter leur retour à la vie civile. Alternant cours théoriques, travaux pratiques et visites de terrain, les stagiaires, composés de militaires et de paramilitaires, se sont familiarisés avec les métiers agropastoraux. Sur le plan agricole, le programme a porté sur l’analyse préalable des sols, la conduite des cultures (céréales, maraîchage et sylviculture), la fertilisation raisonnée, la gestion de l’eau, la protection des végétaux et la conservation des récoltes. Sur le volet pastoral, les modules ont couvert l’élevage de volailles, de bovins, d’ovins et de caprins, incluant l’alimentation, la santé animale, l’habitat et la valorisation des produits transformés, notamment laitiers. À l’issue du cursus, les bénéficiaires ont pris l’engagement d’élaborer chacun un projet professionnel réaliste, adapté à sa région, à ses moyens et à ses compétences. Ils ont promis d’appliquer progressivement les techniques acquises en démarrant à petite échelle, de partager leur savoir-faire avec leurs pairs et de faire preuve de rigueur, d’intégrité et de persévérance dans la gestion de leurs futures exploitations. Plus de 90 militaires formés en agriculture et en élevage pour leur reconversion -©Faso7 S’exprimant au nom des participants, le Colonel-major Soyo Palé a salué cette initiative qui offre une issue concrète vers la vie civile tout en renforçant la sécurité alimentaire. « Dans un pays où l'agriculture et l'élevage font vivre la majorité de la population, former des militaires à ces métiers, c'est mettre à la disposition de la nation des hommes et des femmes disciplinés, endurants, organisés et rompus au sens du devoir », a-t-il déclaré. Pour l’Intendant colonel-major Léonard Yamba Ouoba, cette session constitue un point de départ. Estimant que la reconversion est une priorité et un devoir envers ceux qui ont servi la patrie, il a exhorté les impétrants à passer à l’action en appliquant sur le terrain les acquis de la formation, avec l’objectif de convertir les projets en activités productives et les ambitions en entreprises génératrices de revenus et d’emplois. Les participants se sont familiarisés avec les métiers agropastoraux -©Faso7 « Soyez des ambassadeurs de la reconversion réussie, des producteurs responsables et des entrepreneurs exemplaires. Faites en sorte que votre passage de la vie militaire à la vie civile soit une totale réussite. Il vous appartient désormais de transformer ces acquis en initiatives concrètes, vos projets en activités productives et vos ambitions en entreprises génératrices de revenus et d’emplois » , a-t-il indiqué. À noter que cette formation marque une nouvelle étape dans la réinsertion socioprofessionnelle des personnels des Forces armées nationales en reconversion. items.title: 2027: Obi urges Nigerians to defend their votes
items.description: By Nwabueze Okonkwo ONITSHA — Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, has urged Nigerians to turn out en masse for the January 16, 2027 presidential election and defend their votes against electoral manipulation. Obi made the call on Friday at the NDC town hall meeting and presidential campaign rally held at All Saints Anglican Church Cathedral, Onitsha, Anambra State. He said Nigerians should regard election day as an opportunity to make a sacrifice for the country by coming out to vote and remaining at polling centres to protect their ballots. According to him, whoever emerges winner in a free, fair and transparent election should be supported by all Nigerians. The former Anambra State governor, however, vowed to resist any attempt to manipulate the results in favour of any political party, saying he would not accept a repeat of what he described as irregularities that characterised the 2023 presidential election. “We are going to match them fire for fire if they attempt to rig the election as usual, and we are going to block all loopholes to ensure that our votes count. “The idea is for the right winner to emerge in a free and fair election. Nothing more, nothing less. Personally, I would like to win in a transparent election,” he said. Obi also criticised the borrowing policy of the President Bola Tinubu administration, alleging that trillions of dollars had been borrowed between 2023 and 2026 without sufficient investment in productive sectors of the economy. He warned that another four-year term for the administration after the 2027 election could worsen the country’s economic situation. At the rally, Senator Victor Umeh, representing Anambra Central Senatorial District; NDC candidate for Idemili North/South Federal Constituency, Engr. Eric Anyamene; member representing Onitsha North II in the Anambra State House of Assembly, Hon. Pat Okafor; the party’s Anambra State Deputy Chairman, Barr. Chugbo Enwezor; and Chief Ikenna Victor Egbuna, SAN, expressed confidence that the party would win the presidential, National Assembly and state assembly elections in 2027. items.title: Migrations : Dakar lance un cadre de coopération pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest
items.description: Réunis à l'hôtel Azalaï, les ministres de la région ont ouvert vendredi le segment ministériel d'une conférence appelée à aboutir à une Déclaration de Dakar et à une Feuille de route régionale. Faire de la mobilité humaine un chantier commun plutôt qu'une somme de réponses nationales : c'est le pari du « processus de coopération sur les questions migratoires en Afrique de l'Ouest », officiellement lancé ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026 à Dakar. Les ministres de la région se sont retrouvés à l'hôtel Azalaï pour la phase politique d'une conférence préparée de longue date, en présence de la directrice générale de l'Organisation internationale pour les migrations (OIM), Amy Pope. Retenu hors du territoire par des obligations imprévues, le ministre de l'Intégration africaine, des Affaires étrangères et des Sénégalais de l'Extérieur, Cheikh Niang, a confié l'ouverture des travaux au ministre de la Justice, Garde des Sceaux, Me Moussa Sarr. Devant les chefs de délégation, les diplomates, les organisations régionales et internationales et les partenaires techniques et financiers, ce dernier a d'abord choisi de replacer la question dans le temps long de la région. « Bien avant que nos frontières ne soient tracées, les peuples de l'Afrique de l'Ouest allaient déjà d'un royaume à l'autre, au gré du commerce et de la quête du savoir. La mobilité est inscrite dans notre histoire ; elle a façonné nos familles comme nos cités. Mais lorsque l'espoir d'une vie meilleure se brise au large de nos côtes, elle devient un drame qui interpelle chacun de nos Etats », a-t-il déclaré. Prévention et fermeté face aux passeurs Le ministre a ensuite rattaché la démarche à la politique du chef de l'État, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, dont il a transmis le salut aux participants. « Le Président de la République a fait de la prévention de la migration irrégulière une priorité, en instituant un programme budgétaire spécial qui lui est consacré. Il a également appelé à sanctionner avec sévérité les réseaux de passeurs, ces « marchands d'illusions » qui exposent notre jeunesse à des périls mortels », a-t-il rappelé, avant d'ajouter que la conférence « prolonge cette vision en l'inscrivant dans une démarche régionale ». Cette réunion ministérielle fait suite à deux jours de travaux menés par des experts, des points focaux nationaux et des techniciens, salués par Me Sarr pour leur « rigueur » et leur « détermination ». Leurs échanges ont permis, selon lui, d'établir un diagnostic partagé des dynamiques migratoires de la région. Le ministre a aussi remercié l'OIM, dont l'appui technique et l'expertise ont été « déterminants », des consultations nationales jusqu'à l'organisation de la conférence. Un cadre « durable et évolutif » Pour le Garde des Sceaux, ce processus, engagé il y a plusieurs mois et animé par le Sénégal, traduit une volonté politique claire. « Il répond à la volonté des Etats ouest-africains d'assumer pleinement la gouvernance des migrations, à travers un cadre régional durable et évolutif, fondé sur le dialogue politique et les échanges techniques », a-t-il expliqué. L'objectif, a-t-il précisé, est de « bâtir ensemble un espace de coopération renforcée, capable de rapprocher nos priorités nationales et de favoriser des réponses concertées, adaptées aux réalités de la mobilité dans les pays d'origine, de transit, de destination ou de retour ». Trois priorités se dégagent des travaux des experts : renforcer la gouvernance régionale de la mobilité humaine, protéger effectivement les migrants tout au long des routes migratoires, et valoriser la mobilité comme facteur d'intégration et de développement durable. Elles doivent servir de socle à la Déclaration de Dakar, qui fixera les principes directeurs de la coopération. Une Feuille de route régionale la complétera, en détaillant les actions prioritaires, les responsabilités de chacun ainsi que les mécanismes de suivi et de coordination. Le rôle de la justice Garde des Sceaux, Me Sarr a tenu à souligner la dimension judiciaire du dossier. « La lutte contre le trafic illicite de migrants et la traite des personnes suppose une entraide judiciaire efficace entre nos Etats », a-t-il affirmé, estimant que la pleine efficacité des futurs instruments dépendrait du concours de la justice. Il a conclu son intervention par un appel à passer à l'action : « Il nous revient désormais de traduire ces orientations techniques en réponses politiques collectives, au service d'une migration sûre, ordonnée et régulière, conforme aux aspirations légitimes de nos peuples. »

items.title: St John’s Hospital CEO Dr Maame Yaa Afriye named Outstanding Corporate Woman at 2026 Ghana Women Awards
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of St John’s Hospital and Fertility Centre, Dr Maame Yaa Afriye, has been named Outstanding Corporate Woman at the 2026 Ghana Women Awards. She received the award at a ceremony held at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA) Auditorium on Saturday, November 14, 2026. Dr Afriye was recognised for her leadership and contributions to healthcare management and service delivery. The 2026 Ghana Women Awards brought together 23 women from various sectors, including healthcare, business, entertainment, media, engineering, sports and the security services, to recognise their contributions to society. Other award recipients included the President of the Greater Accra Markets Association, Mercy Naa Afrowa Needjan, who received the Legendary Woman Award, and the Chief Executive Officer of Hasaacas Ladies FC, Dr Evelyn Nsiah Asare, who was named Changemaker of the Year. Dr Afriye is a trained pharmacist with a Bachelor of Science degree in Pharmacy from the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST). She also holds a PhD in Health Policy and Management from the University of Ghana Business School, an MBA in Health Services Management, a Postgraduate Diploma in Business Administration and a Postgraduate Certificate in Supply Chain and Human Resource Management. She has also co-authored research publications on customer relationship management and patient satisfaction, as well as the experiences of working mothers with exclusive breastfeeding in Ghana. As head of St John’s Hospital and Fertility Centre, Dr Afriye has overseen efforts to improve the facility’s operations, infrastructure, technology and patient care. The hospital provides a range of general and specialist healthcare services, including fertility care, urology, surgery, dermatology, dental services, ear, nose and throat (ENT) care, home care and laboratory services. The latest recognition adds to several honours Dr Afriye has received in the healthcare sector. In 2024, she was named Most Outstanding Female in Healthcare and Administrative Excellence at the Corporate Ghana Hall of Fame Awards.

items.title: Ecuador: Latin America & The Caribbean Weekly Situation Update as of 20 November 2026
items.description: Countries: Ecuador, Bolivia (Plurinational State of), El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Peru, United States of America Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached Infographic. KEY FIGURES 7.9K people displaced in Haiti since mid-October 3.2M people could face crisis-level food insecurity in Guatemala 93K people affected by El Niño-related rains in Ecuador HAITI: VIOLENCE & DISPLACEMENT Escalating armed violence across the country is deepening humanitarian needs and restricting access, particularly in densely populated areas of the capital, Port-au-Prince. Since mid-October, violence in Croix-des-Bouquets, on the capital’s outskirts, has displaced about 2,000 people. Nearly 90 per cent are staying with host families and the rest in five informal sites. In late October, attacks in Arcahaie and Cabaret, north-west of the capital, displaced more than 5,900 people. Each new wave puts more strain on stretched host communities. Violence killed an estimated 4,200 people nationwide between January and September, and some 1.5 million people remain displaced. The UN continues to call for the protection of civilians and for safe access to health facilities, schools and other essential services. CENTRAL AMERICA: FOOD SECURITY El Niño-related drought is deepening hunger in Central America’s Dry Corridor, where families are running out of food after a failed harvest. An Oxfam assessment of 354 communities in Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador found that nearly 8 in 10 maize-producing households lost 75 to 100 per cent of their crop this year. Most now have food reserves for three weeks or less. The drought is also cutting rural incomes: the region’s sugar harvest, a key source of seasonal work, could fall by up to 21 per cent. Projections show about 3.2 million people in Guatemala and 1.8 million in Honduras facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels of food insecurity, while up to 249,000 people in El Salvador could face food insecurity. SOUTH AMERICA: EL NIÑO El Niño-related rains are worsening along South America’s Pacific coast. In Ecuador, the number of people affected is 62,000 as of 18 November, up from about 65,000 a week earlier, according to the National Secretariat for Risk Management (SNGR). Of these, 36,729 have lost their homes or livelihoods. The rains have led to 16 deaths, damaged more than 25,600 homes, affected over 2,280 schools and 13,000 hectares of crops, and reached all 24 provinces. The National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI) forecasts heavier rain through 21 November. In northern Peru, overflowing streams have cut off several communities in Tumbes, and forecasters warn the Piura River could rise. On 19 November, authorities placed nine Piura and Tumbes provinces under red alert. REGIONAL: HEALTH ALERTS Measles and malaria are spreading across the region as gaps in immunization and disease control persist. As of 13 November, PAHO had confirmed 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths in the Americas this year, more than four times the number for the same period in 2025. Guatemala accounts for most of them, with more than 34,700 cases and 53 deaths. Bolivia, Mexico and the United States have now lost their measles elimination status. Panama has recorded more than 6,700 malaria cases, mainly in the East Panama, Guna Yala and Darién health regions. They include an outbreak of 161 cases in Ancón, an area of the capital, Panama City, where malaria is not endemic. On 16 November, the Ministry of Health declared a national health alert.

items.title: ‘If a mother’s tears could bring back a child’ – Javits’ mother breaks down during tribute
items.description: The mother of 15-year-old Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits, broke down in tears during the reading of her tribute at his funeral in the Bronx, New York, as she struggled to come to terms with the loss of her only child. The tribute, which was read on her behalf at the funeral on Friday, November 20, recounted her pain over the death of the son she had carried, nurtured and prayed for. Standing beside the reader, Javits’ mother, Doris, became visibly emotional and broke down at the end of the reading. In the message, she described Javits as her only son, her only child and her greatest blessing, saying that although distance separated them when he travelled to the United States to live with his father, their emotional bond remained strong. She recalled their conversations and the dreams he shared with her, particularly his ambition to study hard, become a doctor and one day return to Ghana to take care of her and help less privileged people in their community. “You told me that you wanted to study hard, become a doctor and return one day to take good care of me and help the less privileged in our community in Ghana,” the tribute read. She said those words had become the foundation of her hopes and daily prayers, adding that she had imagined the day she would proudly call him “Doctor”. ‘Mema mo yaakor’ – New York City Major, Zohran Kwame Mamdani, in Akan language, pays tribute to 15-year-old Javits at funeral in the US. Full tribute of @NYCMayor. https://t.co/lu913DMo88 — Kenneth Awotwe Darko (@TheKennethDarko) November 20, 2026 The mother said she had looked forward to watching her son fulfil his ambitions and growing old with the comfort of knowing that he had achieved his dreams. But his death, she said, had abruptly ended a future they had imagined together. “My son, what hurts most is not just that you are gone, but everything you were yet to become. Your dreams, your laughter, your kindness and the beautiful future we imagined together have all been taken away,” she said. In one of the most emotional passages, she expressed the depth of a mother’s grief over the loss. “If a mother’s tears could bring back a child, I would have cried you back into my arms. If love could defeat death, you would still be here,” the tribute read. She ended by assuring her son that he would remain in her heart and that she would carry his dreams and memories for the rest of her life. “Sleep well, my only son. My heart has lost its greatest treasure,” she said. Javits was born on April 29, 2011, and moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to join his father and pursue his education. He aspired to become a doctor and serve in the United States military. He was fatally shot in the Bronx on October 29, 2026, aged 15.

items.title: Ghana’s Education Crossroads: Why Artificial Intelligence must become a tool for inclusive learning and national transformation
items.description: As Ghana prepares to mark National Education Week 2026 on November 23 and 24, attention is increasingly turning to the role artificial intelligence (AI) can play in shaping the future of education. But beyond the excitement surrounding this emerging technology lies a more important question: How can AI improve learning, empower teachers and ensure that no Ghanaian child is left behind? Ghana’s education system is at a defining moment. The world of work is changing, new industries are emerging, and the skills required to participate meaningfully in the global economy are extending beyond traditional academic knowledge. Digital competence, critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving and the ability to work with emerging technologies are becoming increasingly important. Artificial intelligence is at the centre of this transformation. Already, it is changing how people access information, communicate, conduct research and solve problems. For Ghana, the challenge is no longer whether AI will influence education, but how effectively the country can harness its potential while addressing the risks and ensuring that its benefits reach every learner. It is against this background that the Ministry of Education is organising National Education Week 2026 under the theme, “ Harnessing Artificial Intelligence for Inclusive and Transformative Education in Ghana .” Scheduled for November 23 and 24, 2026, at the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission (GTEC), the event will bring together policymakers, educators, researchers, students, development partners, technology experts and other stakeholders to examine how Ghana’s education system can respond to the opportunities and challenges presented by AI. More importantly, the event provides an opportunity to move the conversation beyond simply introducing technology into classrooms and focus on how it can improve the quality, relevance and inclusiveness of education. Beyond Technology: Rethinking the Purpose of Education In his 2025 State of the Nation Address, President John Dramani Mahama emphasised the need for Ghana’s education system to respond to the demands of the 21st century and the Fourth Industrial Revolution. That call reflects the urgency of the moment. For many years, education has largely focused on the transfer of knowledge from teachers to learners. While this remains fundamental, the changing world requires an education system that also equips learners to question information, think independently, apply knowledge and adapt to new circumstances. Artificial intelligence offers opportunities to support this shift. In the classroom, AI-powered applications can help teachers identify areas where learners are struggling, provide additional explanations and tailor learning experiences to individual needs. Students can also access educational resources and explore difficult concepts with greater flexibility. Teachers, on the other hand, can use AI to support lesson preparation, develop teaching materials, assist with assessments and identify learning gaps. School administrators can benefit from data-driven systems that strengthen planning, monitoring and decision-making. At the tertiary level, AI offers opportunities to advance research, encourage innovation and strengthen collaboration between academic institutions and industry. However, the success of this transformation should not be measured by the number of digital devices distributed to schools or the sophistication of the software introduced. What matters most is whether these investments translate into better learning outcomes, expanded opportunities and improved preparation for life and work. Making Inclusion Central to the AI Conversation As Ghana considers the integration of artificial intelligence into education, inclusion must remain a central concern. Technology has the potential to open up new learning opportunities, but without deliberate planning, it could also widen existing inequalities. A learner in an urban school with reliable internet connectivity, access to digital devices and digitally competent teachers may enjoy far greater benefits from AI-supported learning than a child in a rural community where electricity, connectivity and educational resources remain limited. The needs of learners with disabilities must also receive particular attention. AI-enabled accessibility tools, including speech-to-text applications, text-to-speech systems, automated captioning and adaptive learning platforms, can help remove some of the barriers that prevent learners with diverse needs from participating fully in education. However, making these opportunities available will require investment in accessible infrastructure, appropriate learning materials and teacher capacity development. The objective must be to prevent AI from becoming another dividing line between well-resourced and underserved schools. Instead, it should serve as a means of narrowing educational inequalities and extending quality learning opportunities to communities across the country. This is particularly important for Ghana’s national development aspirations, which depend on equipping every child, irrespective of geographical location, economic circumstances or physical ability, with the knowledge and skills to contribute meaningfully to society. The Teacher Remains Central to the Transformation One concern surrounding the growing use of artificial intelligence in education is whether technology will eventually reduce the importance of teachers. Such a concern overlooks the very essence of education. Although AI can process information, generate explanations, identify patterns and provide learning support, teaching involves much more than delivering information. Teachers inspire curiosity, build confidence, encourage discipline, provide emotional support and recognise the individual needs of their learners. They also play a critical role in nurturing the values, judgement and social skills required to develop responsible citizens. These human dimensions of education cannot simply be replicated by technology. Rather than viewing AI as a replacement for teachers, Ghana must position it as a tool that strengthens their professional capabilities and gives them additional resources to support learning. Achieving this will require continuous professional development to help teachers understand how AI works, use it effectively and recognise its limitations. It will also demand changes in teaching approaches, with greater emphasis on critical thinking, creativity, independent inquiry and the responsible use of information. Ultimately, the success of AI integration will depend as much on the preparedness of teachers and other education professionals as it will on the availability of technology. Ghana’s Policy Direction: From Commitment to Implementation Ghana is not starting this journey from scratch. The country has already taken steps towards building a digital economy in which artificial intelligence can contribute meaningfully to national development. In April 2026, President John Dramani Mahama launched Ghana’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy, covering the period 2025–2035. The strategy identifies education, human capital development, research, ethical AI development and workforce readiness as important areas of focus. Government also announced plans for a US$250 million Artificial Intelligence Computing Centre to support research, innovation and the development of local AI solutions. These initiatives reflect the country’s ambition to move beyond merely consuming technology towards building the capacity to develop solutions that respond to its own needs. Within the education sector, there are equally significant developments. In May 2026, the Ministry of Education signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Google for Education to strengthen digital literacy and support the integration of advanced AI technologies into teaching and learning. The partnership is expected to contribute to teacher development, classroom innovation and the acquisition of relevant skills by Ghanaian learners. Another important development is the proposed revision of the basic school curriculum from Kindergarten to Primary Six. Presented to the Minister for Education in July 2026, the revised curriculum incorporates artificial intelligence literacy, computational thinking, coding and digital citizenship, alongside other proposed changes. These additions reflect a growing recognition that learners must begin developing an understanding of technology and its applications from an early age. The curriculum review also recommends a phased and adequately resourced teacher-training programme to support implementation. The Centre for National Distance Learning and Open Schooling (CENDLOS), which provides leadership in open, distance and electronic learning, also has an important role in expanding technology-enabled learning opportunities. Together, these initiatives provide a foundation for the discussions expected at National Education Week 2026. The task ahead is to ensure that these efforts are properly coordinated, adequately resourced and translated into practical improvements across schools and other educational institutions. The Difficult Questions Ghana Must Confront While the opportunities presented by artificial intelligence are considerable, embracing the technology without addressing its risks could undermine the very objectives the education sector seeks to achieve. Unequal access remains one of the biggest concerns. AI-supported learning cannot become a national solution if large numbers of learners and teachers lack electricity, reliable internet connectivity, appropriate devices and the skills required to use them. Other concerns include data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, misinformation and the reliability of information generated by AI systems. There is also the danger of excessive dependence on AI-generated answers. Without proper guidance, learners may become less inclined to conduct independent research, question information or develop their own ideas. Academic integrity presents another important challenge. Educational institutions will need clear guidelines on the acceptable use of AI in assignments, examinations, research and other academic activities. Beyond these concerns is the question of relevance. AI systems developed in other parts of the world may not always reflect Ghana’s educational environment, indigenous languages, cultural values and everyday experiences. This makes it important for Ghana to invest in the development and promotion of technologies that respond to local realities. AI should complement the country’s educational objectives rather than introduce external solutions that may not adequately address local needs. Responsible governance, ethical standards and effective data protection measures must therefore form an essential part of Ghana’s approach to integrating artificial intelligence into education. National Education Week: Moving from Dialogue to Action National Education Week 2026 is expected to provide an important platform for bringing these issues together and translating discussions into practical recommendations. The two-day event will attract a broad range of stakeholders, including policymakers, teachers, school administrators, researchers, academics, student bodies, development partners, civil society organisations, technology providers and traditional authorities. The opening day will feature statements on the state of education in Ghana, the commissioning of an exhibition showcasing digital education initiatives and technical presentations examining the current state of AI adoption and digital technology across the various levels of the education system. The presentations will cover preschool, primary, junior high, secondary, technical and vocational education and training, complementary education, tertiary education and inclusive education. A panel discussion will further provide an opportunity to examine global and African experiences and draw practical lessons for Ghana. The second day will place greater emphasis on research and evidence, offering researchers and institutions the opportunity to present findings on AI adoption and digital education initiatives. This focus on evidence is particularly important. Decisions about technology in education should not be driven solely by enthusiasm or the desire to appear technologically advanced. They must be informed by research, practical implementation experiences, measurable outcomes and a clear understanding of the challenges confronting educational institutions. Technical group discussions will also allow participants to identify priority areas for action and develop recommendations to guide policy and implementation. Among the expected outcomes are policy recommendations aligned with Ghana’s national development agenda, a proposed National AI in Education Roadmap for 2027–2030, stronger partnerships among government and other stakeholders, and an ethical guidelines and data privacy framework for AI in pre-tertiary and tertiary institutions. A draft 2027 Joint Sector Performance Aide-Mémoire is also expected to capture priority commitments on AI and digital technology. These are important ambitions. However, their true value will depend on how effectively the recommendations are implemented, monitored and sustained beyond the event. Collective Responsibility Transforming Ghana’s education system through artificial intelligence cannot be the responsibility of the Ministry of Education alone. Government must provide the policy direction, infrastructure and enabling environment. Educational institutions must be willing to embrace innovation while maintaining academic standards. Teachers must receive the necessary support and training, while parents must understand the changing learning environment and guide their children in using technology responsibly. The private sector also has an important role to play in developing relevant solutions, supporting innovation and investing in digital infrastructure. Development partners, research institutions and civil society organisations must contribute their expertise, evidence and resources to ensure that the transition is inclusive and sustainable. Students, too, must be active participants. Beyond learning how to use AI applications, they must understand how the technology works, question the information it produces, recognise its limitations and apply it responsibly. This calls for a broader understanding of digital education, one that places human development, intellectual independence, creativity and ethical responsibility at its centre. The Future Must Leave No Learner Behind As Ghana prepares for National Education Week 2026, the conversation must extend beyond the technology itself. The more important consideration is the kind of education system the country wants to build and the opportunities it hopes to create for the next generation. A successful AI-driven education system must be one in which a child in a rural community has a meaningful opportunity to benefit from technological advancement; a teacher is empowered rather than displaced by innovation; a learner with a disability can access appropriate learning support; and a university student can use technology to explore new ideas, advance research and contribute to national development. It must also be a system that protects learners, respects their privacy, promotes responsible innovation and recognises that technology is only as valuable as the human purpose it serves. National Education Week 2026 therefore presents Ghana with an opportunity to align its educational ambitions with the realities of a rapidly changing world. Its success will not be determined by the number of presentations delivered, the technologies displayed at exhibitions or even the policies developed. It will ultimately be judged by whether the recommendations lead to better teaching, improved learning outcomes, stronger educational institutions and more equitable opportunities for every Ghanaian child. Artificial intelligence may be shaping the future of education, but the responsibility for determining that future rests with people. Ghana must not simply prepare its learners to live in an AI-driven world. It must equip them with the knowledge, skills and confidence to shape that world. ************ Author: Madeleine Insaidoo, Head PR, Ministry of Education

items.title: 'I would love to see him be back': Trump urges Nvidia to give Jensen Huang 'second chance'
items.description: US President Donald Trump on Friday called for AI giant Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang after he was ousted as CEO over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. “I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go? I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,” Trump told reporters. Huang resigned as chief of the chip giant at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who may have funnelled restricted chips to that country. Earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that Trump did not discuss Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their meeting this week. Responding to a question, Bessent told US broadcaster CNBC that Huang had not come up in Trump’s talks with Xi, held earlier this week in Shenzhen. Speaking about the Trump administration’s support for the domestic AI sector, Bessent stressed that the US “must stay ahead ” of China in that realm. “Our best protection against the foreign SI and exploits by foreign actors is for our labs to maintain their substantial lead, and in effect, they are our shield against SI,” he said, using the administration’s term for AI technology. “There’s no turning back on this. What we have to do is make sure that our labs maintain their leads through their continued innovation, through their access to the best chips, and through smart policy.” Bessent said Trump and Xi had agreed on certain guardrails on the use of AI in the military domain. “President Trump and President Xi agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” he said. On the threat of AI-enabled cyberattacks, Bessent again stressed that the best defence his country had was to allow its AI companies “to continue at the frontier and to provide us with the best defence against these other models”.

items.title: Nearly 600 women killed in South Africa within three months
items.description: Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country’s latest crime statistics. This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg. The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world. In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week. The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg. The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders. Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day. It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were “significant anomalies” in the statistics. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be “greater efforts to prevent… violence” against women and children. According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night. The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, “forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside”, police said. The owner’s wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made. On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year. General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park. Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba’s was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region. He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo’s death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg. Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body. Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area. In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that “no stone will be left unturned” to find those behind the killings. Last year, he declared that violence against women was a “national disaster”.
