Tout refus d’exécution, toute transgression, toute application sélective, incomplète ou à géométrie variable sera sanctionné : le règlement ne restera pas lettre morte ! III) Faire la chasse aux règles tacites. Il faut établir des règles claires et promouvoir la transparence des affaires du Parti et du gouvernement. Il faut que les membres et cadres du Parti soient imprégnés de la nécessité d’observer les principes établis, de respecter la loi et la discipline, de marcher dans la bonne voie et donc de s’opposer aux règles tacites dans l’exercice du pouvoir, la mise en œuvre des politiques, l’obtention d’un projet, la sélection et la nomination des cadres et l’élection d’éléments d’avant-garde. Il faut sévir contre ceux qui cherchent à obtenir des faveurs en recherchant des appuis auprès de leurs supérieurs ou en courtisant les autorités locales, qui pensent que les relations passent avant les principes, qui accordent plus d’importance aux billets qu’aux documents cachetés, qui monnaient leurs services ou qui aiment à manœuvrer en coulisse. Il faut combattre énergiquement la mentalité mercantile et la culture de liens de vassalité, sous peine de voir compromis le fonctionnement interne du Parti. Le système de dénonciation sera amélioré pour que les entremetteurs et les escrocs politiques, ainsi que leurs complices, soient sévèrement punis. Un système d’analyse et d’examen rétrospectif des affaires similaires ainsi que de rectification et de notification sera établi, et l’actuel mécanisme dynamique de surveillance, d’analyse et d’assainissement de l’écosystème politique sera parachevé. Pour poursuivre inlassablement la stricte autogouvernance du Parti sur tous les plans, nous devons continuer à affiner les outils de contrôle dont disposent le Parti et l’État. Nous ferons en sorte que les comités (ou groupes dirigeants) du Parti remplissent effectivement leur tâche de supervision générale, tout en renforçant leur supervision sur les autres entités de contrôle. Le Règlement sur le contrôle interne du Parti sera révisé. Le système de double direction du travail de supervision et de contrôle disciplinaire sera amélioré. La commission de contrôle de la discipline et la commission de supervision de l’échelon supérieur ont la responsabilité principale de diriger les actions de supervision, de contrôle et de poursuite des éléments corrompus, et il faut coordonner les forces disponibles et les rendre plus efficaces. Nous ferons en sorte que soient mieux articulés le contrôle disciplinaire, la supervision, le contrôle exercé par les équipes mandatées à cet effet et les tournées d’inspection. Il convient de mieux utiliser les moyens de contrôle au niveau des districts, des cantons et des villages. Il faut parachever le système de contrôle aux échelons de base, notamment par les contrôles croisés et le recours, en cas de besoin, à une instance de contrôle de niveau plus élevé que l’instance normale. Le contrôle par les masses devra disposer de canaux d’expression plus accessibles. L’administration à la base et le contrôle à la base devront aller de pair. Le contrôle interne du Parti sera combiné avec le contrôle de l’assemblée populaire, le contrôle démocratique, le contrôle administratif, le contrôle judiciaire, le contrôle d’audit, le contrôle de comptabilité, le contrôle de statistiques, le contrôle des masses et le contrôle par l’opinion, de manière à ce qu’ils interagissent efficacement et forment une synergie. Nous appliquerons sur tous les plans les principes de travail relatifs aux tournées d’inspection du Parti et concrétiserons les règlements dans ce domaine. Nous tirerons le meilleur parti possible des inspections, qu’elles soient régulières, spéciales ou circonstancielles et nous n’hésiterons pas à recourir au besoin à une instance hiérarchique d’un niveau supérieur à l’instance de tutelle normale. Les méthodes d’inspection seront rénovées, les inspections « rétrospectives » seront intensifiées, le suivi des inspections sera amélioré et l’utilisation des résultats obtenus, optimisée. Nous favoriserons l’interaction verticale des missions d’inspection de différentes hiérarchies, et améliorerons la qualité et l’efficacité des inspections effectuées dans les villages. Bref, il faut que les tournées d’inspection deviennent véritablement le fer de lance de notre effort de contrôle général. Poursuivre inlassablement l’autogouvernance intégrale du Parti avec rigueur est la responsabilité politique commune de tout le Parti. Il faut concentrer nos efforts sur l’application du système de responsabilité, car celui-ci joue un rôle clé dans l’autogouvernance du Parti. Pour rappel : le comité (ou groupe dirigeant) du Parti assume la responsabilité principale ; la commission de contrôle de la discipline assume la responsabilité de supervision ; le secrétaire du comité (ou groupe dirigeant) du Parti agit en tant que premier responsable, le reste des membres remplissant un double devoir ; les membres et cadres du Parti ont chacun leurs propres responsabilités. Il s’agit de bien faire fonctionner ce système unifié et coordonné où chacun assume ses responsabilités. Les comités (ou groupes dirigeants) du Parti à tous les échelons doivent y veiller avec zèle en resserrant la chaîne des responsabilités et en faisant passer les pressions d’un niveau à l’autre. Les comités (ou groupes dirigeants) du Parti au niveau du district et au-dessus doivent écouter, au moins une fois par an, les comptes rendus de leurs membres dirigeants sur la manière dont ils se sont acquittés de leur tâche de gouvernance du Parti, en leur offrant aide et encouragements au besoin. Les commissions de contrôle de la discipline à tous les échelons (ou équipes de contrôle disciplinaire et de supervision envoyées sur place) sont tenues de remplir dûment leurs responsabilités : tous les six mois au moins, chaque instance soumettra à l’instance supérieure un rapport qui porte sur la manière dont l’équipe dirigeante du comité du Parti, notamment son « numéro un », se sont acquittés de leurs responsabilités et ont exercé leurs attributions, ainsi que sur la manière dont elle a elle-même rempli sa tâche de contrôle et de supervision. Chaque branche du comité du Parti doit remplir comme il se doit ses responsabilités tout en coopérant avec les autres. Les cadres dirigeants, surtout les plus hauts dirigeants, sont tenus d’être particulièrement exigeants envers eux-mêmes, d’assumer avec le plus grand sérieux leurs responsabilités uniques, d’exercer le contrôle le plus strict sur toutes les activités qui relèvent de leur compétence et de donner l’exemple d’une impeccable gouvernance du Parti. En menant à bien le renforcement du Parti à tous les niveaux et dans tous les domaines, nous devons toujours faire preuve d’objectivité et chercher à obtenir des résultats réels, en évitant tout formalisme. Il convient d’ailleurs d’améliorer le système d’évaluation afin de vérifier comment chaque cadre s’acquitte de ses tâches dans le domaine de la gouvernance du Parti. Tout manquement, toute faute grave sur ce plan seront sévèrement punis. L’histoire laisse entrevoir l’aube de l’avenir, l’effort est le prix de tout grand projet. Dans sa marche impétueuse, le Parti communiste chinois s’est forgé de nombreuses qualités : il a acquis la détermination de poursuivre sans relâche la vérité et de toujours suivre le bon cap ; il s’est profondément enraciné dans le peuple, se dotant de la meilleure base qui soit ; il a eu le courage d’assumer sa mission historique et s’est assuré l’initiative sur le plan stratégique ; épousant l’élan du développement qui anime le monde, il s’est propulsé à l’avant-garde de notre temps et y est resté ; il a eu l’audace et la force de combattre, ne doutant jamais de l’issue du combat ; il n’a jamais négligé de se rendre plus fort et n’a donc jamais perdu sa vitalité. Les vicissitudes et les immenses changements qui ont eu lieu sur la terre de Chine pendant plus d’un siècle ont démontré que le Parti est digne de la mission que l’Histoire lui a confiée et de la confiance du peuple, et qu’il mérite absolument d’être le détachement d’avant-garde de la classe ouvrière, du peuple et de la nation chinoise. Le grand, glorieux et juste Parti communiste chinois, en dépit des vents et tempêtes qui l’ont secoué, n’a jamais renié les idéaux de sa jeunesse, avançant courageusement et d’un pas ferme vers ses objectifs. Ayant constamment à l’esprit le « triple impératif » et toujours prêt à présenter lucidement sa copie à l’examen du pouvoir, il n’hésitera pas à livrer une grandiose lutte aux nombreuses caractéristiques nouvelles, et renforcera sa détermination à bâtir un avenir meilleur en surmontant toutes les difficultés ! L’heure est venue de nous unir plus étroitement au Comité central du Parti rassemblé autour du camarade Xi Jinping, et d’appliquer dans son intégralité la pensée de Xi Jinping sur le socialisme à la chinoise de la nouvelle ère, pour que tout le Parti travaille sans relâche et avec acharnement à la poursuite de l’autogouvernance rigoureuse du Parti sur tous les plans, de sorte que s’ouvrent de nouvelles perspectives au contrôle, à la gouvernance, au développement et au renforcement du Parti sous la nouvelle ère. Unissant et conduisant le peuple chinois multiethnique dans une lutte incessante, nous ferons ensemble de la Chine un grand pays socialiste moderne dans tous les domaines et promouvrons intégralement le grand renouveau de la nation grâce à la modernisation chinoise ! L’article Xi Jinping a-t-il rendu son pouvoir éternel ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: What’s So Important About Nvidia’s Chips?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the advanced chips powering the AI boom. But what exactly are these chips, and why do they matter? Ben Buchanan was one of President Biden’s AI advisers and helped write some of the U.S. policies on chip controls, in conversation with people like Huang. In this episode of Galaxy Brain , he breaks down what makes those chips so valuable and why they have such implications for the U.S.-Chinese relationship and the future of AI. The following is a transcript of the episode: Ben Buchanan: We had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. [ Music ] Charlie Warzel: The further we get out from the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal, the more it seems clear that, despite all the salacious details, there’s a lot more to this story than meets the eye. It’s an alleged Chinese-spy sex scandal, yes. It’s the fall of a tech giant. It’s this huge, Silicon Valley palace-intrigue story. But as time goes by, it seems that the epicenter of this story is in Washington, D.C. The Nvidia–Jensen Huang affair is, at heart, a geopolitical thriller. It is a series of cascading events that’s been set in motion by a cold war between China and the United States over advanced AI chips and the AI race. And so to really understand why Huang had to resign, why he’s being called before Congress to testify, why the SEC has reportedly launched a probe into Nvidia—you have to understand how the U.S. got locked in this AI race with China, and how Nvidia’s chips work to power the AI boom. You have to understand the policies that have led to the export restrictions on the chips that Nvidia sells, and the convoluted loopholes that Nvidia and Alice Huang have allegedly used to get chips into China. And my guest today: He not only understands every element of this story; he helps shape it. Ben Buchanan is the former White House special adviser on AI during the Biden administration. Buchanan helped design the chip-export controls on China that Huang and Nvidia lobbied against. And along with Tantum Collins, he’s the author of this new book, The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World . He was in the room for so many of the events that led to where we are now. And today, he’s going to help us mere mortals actually understand what the heck is going on with China, chips, Jensen Huang, the AI race, and crucially, why all of it matters. He joins me now. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Ben Buchanan, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Ben Buchanan: Thanks for having me. Warzel: So I’m hoping in this interview that we could do some very basic questions that will lead to this deeper understanding of the U.S.-China race, the labs; what’s going on. But first I just want to ask about Jensen Huang. Have you taken what we know now and reexamined any of either the interactions you’ve had with him or his company? Like, were there things in retrospect that now that look like signs of vulnerability? How are you processing this news moment, given your relationship to this entire story? Buchanan: For background, I was the White House special adviser for AI and worked in the National Security Council, and was the architect of a lot of the chip controls that seem to be at the crux of this story here. In the course of doing that work for four years, we had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. Certainly about the importance of chips to national security, the importance of AI to national security, and the necessity to cut off smuggling routes and remote access routes for China to get access to that technology. So, in some sense, it’s like a new chapter in a long-running novel. Maybe a particularly salacious and interesting chapter. But it fits the themes of the novel that I’ve lived, I guess now for six years. Warzel: Some of this stuff, especially. And I want to get into the stuff about Megaspeed: the company that Huang’s alleged mistress, and alleged Chinese intelligence asset, worked for. That’s in your book. Megaspeed is in your book. And so I’m just curious. Like, was all this on your radar, and you were expecting it all to come out in some fashion? Or were you pretty shocked by the fact that we’re all talking about this right now? Buchanan: I never knew of the sex thing. As best I can recall, I did not know of Megaspeed in the government. I definitely don’t think I ever heard the name Alice Huang. Megaspeed is in the book because The New York Times did a good story on it 13 or 14 months ago. And it looked to us, when we were writing the book, as a great avatar or example of exactly the kind of smuggling and remote access we were worried about, and we were trying to prevent. While the particulars of this case are new to me, or at least were not something we discussed in the government, the general idea of circumvention of the export controls because this technology is so important was something that we spent a lot of time on and in fact were actively trying to combat. Warzel: So I wanna ask some basic questions here, because I imagine I’m not alone in what is essentially like a pretty shallow understanding of the story in Nvidia. I think, you know, reading the news, a lot of people understand they make advanced AI chips, power the boom we’re experiencing here. They have an extraordinary amount of market share. But walk me through just to set the table here. Like, why is that? What makes Nvidia’s chips so great, so necessary, such a fundamental part of this whole boom? Buchanan: I would look at Nvidia as a key part of maybe the world’s most advanced supply chain and manufacturing process. So Nvidia designs the chips that are incredibly intricate—hundreds of billions of transistors at nanometer scale—that enable this AI revolution that we’re part of, for better or for worse. And those chips are made in Taiwan almost exclusively at TSMC using equipment from ASML in the Netherlands. These are three companies we profile in a lot of detail in the book, because they’re three of the most important companies in the world. Everyone knows of Nvidia; some people know of TSMC; almost no one knows of ASML. But it’s that kind of supply chain, and then all their subcontractors from there, that is at the core of AI. In AI, we have this notion called the bitter lesson , which is the inspiration for the book’s title, The Bitter Struggle . And the bitter lesson is that AI scientists want to make AI systems almost in this divine-creation process, in which they’re handcrafting the algorithms to perfectly mimic or encapsulate human knowledge. But actually, what works much better, we’ve observed, is giving the systems a flexible algorithm from which to learn. A lot of computing power. And getting out of the way. And that’s why it’s computing power—and in particular these days, Nvidia’s chips—that are at the absolute forefront of this AI story, and therefore this geopolitical story. Because what companies have realized is they can scale up the amount of computing power. They can scale up the amount of Nvidia chips that are used to make AI systems, and they get much more powerful systems as a result. In a very predictable fashion. And that, more than any other single factor, I think, has been the tailwind that’s propelled AI progress over the last 10 or 15 years. Warzel: And it’s what’s made them these companies just basically insatiable, right? In terms of how much they want to purchase. How much they want to use. Buchanan: That’s right. Yeah, it’s worth dwelling, for one second, just on the numbers here. Because they’re absolutely mind blowing. And they underscore one of the other important elements in the book and in our policy—which is that AI is the first revolutionary technology of the last hundred or so years that comes from the private sector. Think about nukes and space, and so much else, coming from the government. The government’s cutting the checks at a minimum, and has some capacity to steer where the technology goes. The modern paradigm of AI, this computing power–driven paradigm that we were just talking about, comes from the private sector. And it really is just eye-popping: the amount of investment the private sector is making in pursuit of the bitter lesson, or what’s sometimes called the scaling law. In 2026 alone, the estimates are that the hyperscalers, the big compute companies, will spend $700 billion on infrastructure and growing to a trillion or so dollars by 2027. Just taking the 2026 number, that’s akin to a Manhattan Project basically every two or three weeks. That’s more than America spent building the entire interstate-highway system, adjusting for inflation over 35 years. So it’s just so hard to overestimate the amount of computing power at play here in making these AI systems. Warzel: And it sets the stakes of this, I think, extremely well. Before we get into the nuts and bolts of this Nvidia story, I wanna step back; talk to a little bit about our technological relationship to China. You’ve said in the book, in the past, that AI will be the fulcrum on which the U.S.-China rivalry turns. So help me understand why that is. And also why it’s so bad that China gets access to these chips. Buchanan: We entered the White House in 2021 with the belief that AI would become very relevant, if not at the absolute center, of national-security affairs. Not just with China, but around the world. There’s a number of ways in which that importance could manifest over time, which we thought would take five or so years. Let’s take the one that’s the most concrete right now, and that’s cyber operations. It’s no secret that the United States and China engage every single day in cyber operations; cyber espionage against one another. That this is one of the key contours of competition between the two nations—that if you have an advantage in cyber operations, you have a substantial national-security advantage. I don’t think anyone can test that at this point. What was speculative in 2021—but that we believed would come to pass before too long—was that AI would change cyber operations. In 2026, it has. In 2026 alone, AI systems have discovered thousands, if not tens of thousands, of critical vulnerabilities in vital software all over the internet. The AI companies that have built this software, working in concert with the U.S. government, have turned these vulnerabilities over to vendors and to other network defenders, so that they can be patched and remediated. Essentially making the internet as a whole more secure. My belief, and I think this is pretty well supported, is that if China had access to such a technology and was finding these kinds of vulnerabilities in software, it would not be turning them over to be fixed and remediated. It would be using them for intelligence purposes. And that would put key parts of American critical infrastructure at risk. Just recently, this past week, as we’re recording this here, an AI company using an advanced AI system disclosed that they had found a vulnerability in Java, one of the absolute core languages that makes the modern economy go. A couple of weeks ago, the same company announced that they found a vulnerability in PHP, which is the back end for 70 percent of the websites on the internet. So we are talking about mega-vulnerabilities that AI systems are finding that have profound national-security implications in the wrong hand. And our view was certainly that it was better for the United States to get to that threshold first. Warzel: So you’ve also said that this race to unlock all these capabilities, including the cyber capabilities, may be “winner take all,” I think is how you described it. Help me understand why that’s a zero-sum game. Buchanan: I think we should be very precise here. So the dynamics are close to winner take all—which is to say, if you get to these critical thresholds first, then you can aggregate for yourself a lot of the power that comes from reaching those thresholds. We just gave the cyber example. I think there’s no doubt that the nation that got there first has a lot of power. What you choose to do with that power does not need to be zero sum. And in fact, I would argue throughout American history, a lot of the moments where American policymaking was at its best was when it had a fair amount of power and in some ways ceded that power to institutions, or built a stabilizing framework. So I don’t know that it’s zero sum in the geopolitical sense. Certainly, when I was in the government, we spent a lot of time trying to negotiate with China. And trying to say to China: Look, we’re taking competitive actions here, of course. But we think there’s interest, and that both of us have, that are shared. Let’s work on making this a positive-sum relationship. The Chinese largely blew us off. We can talk about it if you’d like. But this was certainly a key part of our overall AI strategy. Warzel: How would you describe the “they blew us off” part of that? Buchanan: So in October 2023, President Biden signed an executive order that included a line that when you translate from the legalese, essentially, said the United States will engage on AI safety—not just with its allies and its partners, but with its competitors. And that of course meant China. And President Biden personally took that line to President Xi [Jinping] three weeks later when the two leaders met in Woodside, California. And essentially he said: I’m serious about this. We have to work together on this and have a positive-sum relationship . The two leaders agreed to set up a dialogue of the AI experts in Geneva in May of ’24. It happened. I was there. It was maybe 10 or so U.S.-government officials, 10 or so Chinese-government officials. We took it incredibly seriously. We sent essentially everyone who was an AI leader in the U.S. government, went on this trip. The Chinese did not. And the Chinese subordinated it to their political apparatus, and spent the entire meeting essentially saying, like: We’re not sure why you’re talking about risks. We don’t see risks in AI. All this discussion of risks, even shared risks, is American imperialism. We pushed anyway. And we said, No, we really think there’s shared risks here. We really think there’s things we can do that are positive sum. Eventually, after six months of pushing on that point, we got the most common-sense thing, the thing that you should think would take six minutes. And that was an agreement between the two leaders, President Biden and President Xi, when they met for the last time, in November 2024—to not put AI in nuclear command and control. And I think we can all agree we don’t want AI firing nuclear weapons. So this should be the most simple thing in the world, but it took 13 months of pushing to get China to even get there. I’m hopeful China’s posture is different now. Certainly if we had had a second term, we would have—we were making plans to continue outreach to China on this point. But there wasn’t a lot of doubt in my mind that China was not, at the time, ready to have a serious conversation about shared interests and shared risks, and how we could all work together. Warzel: Do you have any sense of where you think China sits now on this? Given that, you know, the capabilities have skyrocketed? This is clearly a more of a top-of-mind geopolitical issue probably than it was, you know, during the Biden administration. Buchanan: I can point to some pieces of evidence that suggests China’s taking it more seriously. There’s some suggestion they’re thinking about cyber risks and talking to their companies about cyber risks. There’s some suggestion in some of the Chinese Communist Party publications that they’re warning about the dangers of AI and so forth. So I think there’s some evidence. And certainly, those are the threads I would be pulling if I were in the government. But also, China is essentially a nation run by one person. And I think it’s very hard, you know, even when you have access to U.S. intelligence to know exactly what Xi Jinping is thinking. I don’t have access to U.S. intelligence right now. So I wouldn’t wanna pretend to know what’s in his head when it comes to AI. And that, really, at the end of the day is the ultimate question when it comes to China. [ Break ] Warzel: So the Biden White House has a, you know, very specific policy about China having access to Nvidia’s chips. There’s a real focus on this amongst all the AI-policy folks, including yourself. Take me to [Jensen] Huang and Nvidia. What is Huang’s policy toward China when it comes to selling to them or around this period? Buchanan: He said the same thing in private that he said in public. Which is, we put this policy in place in 2022. We said to him, essentially: The supply of chips in the world is fixed, because it’s so hard to make them. There’s not gonna be that many more coming off the line. And we want those chips to not go to China. Because we’re worried they’re gonna modernize their military; they’re gonna repress their population with these surveillance tools and the like. Instead, we want those chips to go to the rest of the world, but especially companies in democratic nations. And Nvidia’s posture was that this would really hurt them; that this was bad for them economically. And that they needed the China market in order to compete. And sometimes, to give the sort of steel man of Jensen’s position, Jensen would often say things like—or Jensen and, I should say, his supporters, because there’s a whole group of folks who had this view—would say things like: Well, we need to keep China dependent on American chips. And we’ve got to sell them the chips, so they don’t make their own. We disagreed with the two prongs of that argument. The first prong we disagreed with was that this would be very bad for Nvidia. And essentially, our view was that the bitter lesson that we talked about before was so dominant, that the tailwinds of demand for American compute—I think you said the companies in the United States are insatiable when it comes to compute. That’s absolutely right. Jensen said that as well. And they would buy every single chip Nvidia made, and they would buy it for a significant profit. And that’s exactly what happened. Nvidia’s market capitalization in 2022, when we did the controls, was something like $350 billion. Just before the Jensen scandal a couple of weeks ago, it was $5 trillion. They’ve had a rough week here. But depending on how you do the math, they’re probably up 10 or 15 X on where they were when the compute control started, because of the tailwind that we foresaw about the scaling law and the bitter lesson and the demand for compute. So Nvidia has done great. And in fact, on the Nvidia earnings call just this week, when asked about a recent Trump action to close some of these loopholes and reassert export controls, they downplayed the impact of it, because they’re now acknowledging the demand is so big around the world. So we don’t think we were hurting Nvidia. We think Nvidia was going to do very well under our policy, and indeed they did. The second question is: Are we hurting the United States? Because, do the chip controls cause China to indigenize production in a way they wouldn’t otherwise have? And therefore we lose some leverage over China because they’re no longer dependent on American chips? I also think this was wrong, and we thought it was wrong at the time. The reason why is that China knew the importance of advanced chips. As far back as 2014, when America was off fighting ISIS, China recognized, up to the Xi Jinping level and the State Council of China, recognized how important chipmaking was. China at the time was spending more money importing chips than it was spending importing oil. And they couldn’t make any advanced chips at home. So Xi Jinping began an effort when you count the public and private capital upwards of $200 billion to build a chipmaking industry in China. So they had the pedal to the metal on indigenization before we ever took any action. The Trump administration, in their first term, made it a little bit harder. They cut China off the top end of equipment called EV machines—from the company I mentioned before, ASML. And then when we took the controls, we put the controls in place in 2022 on chips. We also put controls in place on chipmaking equipment, another generation of chipmaking equipment, which were imperfect, but what held China back. So the bottom line is even today, even despite the controls and despite China’s more than a decade-long effort to indigenize, chipmaking is so hard that China has failed. And don’t take my word for it: [Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick, one of the men at the center of this recent export-control story, testified in 2025 China can make just 200,000 chips. And together, 200,000 for the whole country is not nearly enough. It’s not even enough for a single data center. So those were Nvidia’s arguments, and what our responses were to them. Warzel: So in 2022, as you said, the U.S. implements these pretty sweeping export controls on semiconductors or on the chips. Can you briefly explain to me that policy in broad source for people who are not familiar with, you know, the export controls? Buchanan: Basically, our view was the risk of diversion was so high—that the chips could be sold to a civilian buyer, but would end up in PLA, the Chinese-military data centers, or end up in the domestic surveillance apparatus—that we had to control the sale of chips. Not just to the particular military buyers in China, but to the whole country. So the policy in 2022, and then some tightenings thereafter, was to say to companies like Nvidia: You may not sell your product; these advanced chips. You can sell lower-end chips, but you cannot sell these particular advanced chips into China, full stop . And that was a big step. Warzel: This is a dumb question, but what’s the penalty there? Buchanan: It’s a crime. The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have together pursued investigations to arrest and charge people who have violated U.S. export controls or smuggled chips into China, or things like that. Warzel: So the export controls, as I know it in the story, is ultimately one of the decisions that brings Huang and Nvidia—who are not, you know, huge political players leading up to this—more into the D.C. fold, right? It seems that a lot of like their advocacy, especially Huang’s, really ramps up in response to this. So I’m curious: Tell me how Nvidia started rolling up its sleeves and lobbying against those bans starting around 2022, when you guys put them in. Buchanan: We consulted with Nvidia as we were doing it, even before it happened. Because we were trying to understand the technology, and we were certainly not trying to surprise them out of the blue. So it’s not like they woke up one morning and said, Well, you know, the policy is in effect right now. So there were conversations all along. I think those conversations obviously intensified once the policy was in effect, and as we were making adjustments to it and so forth. But these were the reasonably standard conversations that the government has with companies. And you know, when I was the White House special adviser for AI, I talked to all the AI companies pretty regularly. I think it’s part of the job of the government, especially when the private sector is inventing the technology. It’s part of the job of the government to understand what they’re doing, and what its implications are. Warzel: But I’m curious. Like the tenor, the tone of it—as someone who had the opportunity to be in the room. I’ve seen some reports. There’s a report that I read recently from Semafor about Nvidia’s more recent lobbying efforts. Quoting an anonymous congressional staffer saying their MO has been largely gaslighting: creating an intense trust deficit between government, the Hill, and Nvidia. Like, were these conversations acrimonious? What’s the tenor of these conversations? Buchanan: I think they were strident, maybe even aggressive, but it didn’t bother me. I don’t—you know, I just felt like Jensen was doing his job, and talking his book. And those of us in the White House, and they were a group of us in the White House who had very strong conviction on this, felt like we were here to serve U.S. national security. And serve the public, and also serve American innovation. But we certainly felt like we had the technical depth to have detailed conversations with Nvidia, and we did. And you know, the policy ended where, I think, in general the policy should have ended. I would have probably been a little bit more aggressive, if you had asked me, in terms of some of the controls. But in general, I think the policy got to where it needed to be. Probably got there slower than it needed to get there. But in general, I’m happy with certainly our core strategic and technological thesis, which I think has been borne out at this point. Warzel: So now we’re at the current scandal. The affair with Alice Huang—no relation, and former executive at Megaspeed. Allegedly the Chinese intelligence asset. With the caveat that Megaspeed has denied all allegations of wrongdoing, can you explain a little bit about how this alleged chip smuggling works in practice? Buchanan: So I want to be clear here that I don’t have firsthand knowledge of Megaspeed. I’m only going off the news reports. I’ve left the U.S. government, obviously, in January 2025. But it does seem like Megaspeed is an exemplar of two categories of risk that worried us quite a bit when it comes to China’s access to chips. The first is that the chips themselves would be smuggled into China. So they would be purchased in a place like Malaysia or Singapore. There might be some facade of a buyer, potentially a company like Megaspeed in one of those places, that is taking the chips into their data center; is saying, Yes, we’re going to run them here. Everything is good. Don’t worry. And then they’re taking the chips out of the data center, and they’re shipping them into China. And they’re ending up in a Chinese-military data center or the data center of a company that works for the Chinese military, or something like that. And that obviously is a very significant concern for the United States, because that’s direct smuggling of the chips themselves. And we don’t know—once they go into China, we don’t know what the chips are going to be used for. The second category of concern is what’s called remote access. The chips still go to a kind of shady company in Malaysia or Singapore, or a place like that. They go into a data center, but they stay there. The difference is China—Chinese military, Chinese companies—just access that data center remotely over the internet. So the chips stay there, but China can train their next-frontier AI system on this data center, remote. So it’s a different way of circumvent export controls. And we made a decision in one of the export-control updates to try to block that. To say: As a condition of taking these chips, you have to pledge that you will not use them to enable Chinese AI training. President Trump, when he came into office, declined to enforce that rule. So there’s at least a legal gray space—of maybe it was permitted, or the administration wasn’t enforcing it. But those are the two big categories of concern: the actual physical smuggling of the chip, and then the remote access. It’s worth saying Nvidia spent a great deal of time in 2025 and 2026, including Jensen personally, saying chip smuggling is not an issue. And I think it’s obviously incorrect. Not just because of the Megaspeed case, but also because of other cases in which the Department of Justice has brought really well-documented indictments and criminal charges against people for smuggling chips in the way that I described. Warzel: In terms of that remote access to those data centers that are outside of China, for training purposes, it’s known that China has distilled—or sort of reverse-engineered, you know—U.S. models in order to kind of keep up in the race here. Is that where that is happening in your mind? Like, inside those places? Or is that happening more locally? Or is it a mix of the two? Buchanan: Assume it’s a mix. So let’s just be very precise about what’s happening. Distillation is a process in which you can essentially—you know, if folks here are Formula 1 fans, you can draft behind the car in front of you. And you can get the outputs of a leading AI system and come up with the facsimile of that system, imperfectly. You’ll lag capabilities, but it’s cheaper. That is a general concern. And one of the ways in which China has been trying to compensate for the lack of computing power. Essentially, is copying the Americans’ homework. That process of distillation still requires some computing power. And I would imagine China is using whatever computing power it has available to do the process of distillation, whether that’s chips overseas or chips in China. Companies have gotten much better at stopping distillation. So Anthropic, a company that I advise, but I don’t speak for, reported that they came up with methods in the summer of 2026 to stop distillation. I think it was like up to like 99 percent. And I think OpenAI is making some moves in that direction as well. So my suspicion, hard to know for sure, is that we will look at this kind of adversarial distillation as an artifact of a period from 2025 to 2026 where China really struggled with access to computing power, in part due to the export controls, and was using distillation as a way to try to keep up with the frontier. But I don’t think that will be sustainable for them in the long run. And then they’ll be back to the same box of not having enough computing power. [ Break ] Warzel: Given what we’ve learned about Megaspeed, and what you’ve said about the Department of Justice also bringing cases about people trying to, you know, navigate around these export controls—what is your sense of just how much Nvidia helped China get access to these chips? Like, how bad is this going to get for Jensen, for Nvidia, in terms of where this can go? Buchanan: It’s a great question. Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the facts here, and I don’t want to pretend. It does seem like the amount of chips going through these channels was really significant, potentially even more than the number of chips China could make as a whole country itself. I think The Wall Street Journal reported something like $12 billion of chips. I’ve seen other reportings saying it was $4 billion to $5 billion of chips. Megaspeed is just one company. There were other companies that were potentially doing this. What Nvidia knew, what Jensen knew—that is all for congressional and maybe criminal investigators to find out. I don’t pretend to know. But certainly, as a national-security matter, I do think that the flow of chips to China in this way—smuggling and through remote data centers—is one of the biggest national-security weaknesses the United States has. And what you’ve seen really is a pretty clear bipartisan consensus to change the policy. And there’s bipartisan bills in the Congress—introduced by, you know, MAGA senators like Tom Cotton and Jim Banks, and people like that—that would cut China off chips and chipmaking equipment as a matter of law. So the president couldn’t change it, even if he wanted to. And then, even the Trump administration, this past Monday, changed their policy and cut off remote access to data centers and required licenses for shipments to Southeast Asia to try to cut off the smuggling. They’re not quite done; there’s still a couple loopholes in their rule. But that was a very significant action for an administration that really, you know, from the middle of 2025 to today, was only taking export controls away and not enforcing them, rather than putting them into practice. Warzel: So there are calls from Silicon Valley right—from the shareholders, from the, you know, VC types, the other tech founders of some esteem. They want Jensen Huang to come back. He’s a visionary; he’s integral to the AI economy . Help me understand the rationale here, because China is enemy No. 1 in terms of the race to superintelligence. But also, it just seems like they’re abandoning the China fears all of a sudden, or excusing this dalliance. This potential dalliance. Buchanan: I think a lot of the folks who are making those calls—which, to be clear, the Nvidia board pretty clearly rejected on their earnings call this week. A lot of that constellation of people has been pretty dismissive of the China concern. So they’re often the ones supporting selling chips to China. So at least they’re consistent on that front, in that they’re just not worried about this. I think there’s probably a key difference between my view and their view. Which is: I think AI really is going to matter for national security. And at least their revealed preference is they don’t think that, because they’re willing to let China in the game. But as a national-security matter, I certainly am very concerned and think these activities should be investigated. Warzel: What is so hard for me to understand with that is that the national-security imperative is part of the imperative of the companies, that are saying: We can’t afford to truly pace the frontier— or “stop” or “pause” or whatever —because it’s imperative that we beat China to this. I mean, I do feel like they’re speaking out of both corners of their mouth here. Buchanan: I do think, yeah. So if what you’re saying is sometimes the same people who are saying We can’t regulate AI are also saying Let’s sell chips to China. I mean: We can’t regulate AI, because we have to beat China are also saying Let’s sell chips to China . I agree. That is totally incoherent. It doesn’t make any sense to me. President Trump himself—in, you know, militaristic terms that I would not use, given our discussion before about how we hope to have a positive-sum outcome here—President Trump is very fond of saying: Whoever wins AI, wins . You would think if that is your policy, you would not want to sell chips to China. I don’t get it. I think it’s incoherent for the reason you describe. To be clear about what I do believe, my view is: American companies in fact do have to slow down. And I support pacing the frontier. We haven’t talked about it, but you know, part two of the book is all about how we regulated the AI companies, and what more we need to do on the regulation side. That was sort of huge part of our policy. And my view is that, in fact, the way in which we can create the space for regulation—as far back as 2021, we believed—was to slow China down. And China’s absolute dependence on American computing power was a way for us to slow China down, to build a lead for the United States. And then to, if you’d like, spend that lead on safety, to when the technology got to a critical moment. Which is what we’re in right now. To regulate the companies pretty aggressively, if I had my way. To make sure this technology is safe before it’s rolled out. Without this argument of: Well, we’re in an arms race with China; we must forge ahead . Which I thought was just very destructive. Warzel: So where does this all leave us right now, as we’re sitting in the story here? We’re talking Wednesday, November 18th. Obviously, things are changing by the minute. Buchanan: Always good to timestamp these conversations, ’cause it’s been changing every 24 hours. Warzel: Genuinely, it is. How much hot water is Jensen in? How dangerous and serious is this for Nvidia, as Huang goes to testify before Congress in December? Like, what are the stakes for both Huang and Nvidia going forward? Buchanan: I think they’re very high. Congress, in a bipartisan way, said it’s gonna do an investigation here. I don’t know what’s gonna turn up, but certainly they’ve got a lot of threads to pull. Whether or not there’s a criminal investigation, I have no idea. But I do suspect there will be a lot of government investigations into what happened here, and there should be. I guess in the medium term, Nvidia’s chips are still gonna be really good, and there’s still gonna be big demand for them. So as long as Nvidia can keep making great products, I think they will continue to sell those products. I guess it’s an open question of: Can they make great products without Jensen? We’ll see. They’ve got 31,000 research engineers, or something like that. So there’s a lot of smart people there, and they’ve got a lot of great technology. So we’ll see what happens to them technologically. But yeah; in the context of the investigations, certainly I would describe this as a serious moment. Warzel: What should senators be asking? Or what should anyone in Congress be asking Huang when he’s up there, you know, in front of Congress? Buchanan: It’s the most important, age-old question in any kind of D.C. investigation, which is: What did you know, and when did you know it? And they should be asking Jensen that, and they should be asking the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, that. Who knew what about where these chips were going. Who was getting them. How active was Nvidia’s role in enabling smuggling? How active was Jensen’s role? Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the answers. But those were all the questions I’d be asking. Warzel: And I think lastly here, what has this done for the AI ecosystem right now? Like, is it in a worse place than it was? Or let’s just say, the American AI ecosystem? Is it in a worse place than it was two weeks ago, before all of this stuff really trickled out into the press? Or it was about the same? Buchanan: I think it probably creates some turbulence in the waters, but my suspicion is we’ll look back at this in six or 12 months, and the big story of AI will be largely unchanged by this. And the big story of AI, you know—as we spent a lot of detail on the book—is: You have really powerful chips being used by really capable algorithms, at larger and larger scales. Yielding extraordinarily capable systems, with profound national-security implications and profound implications for everyday life and democratic values. That story. To be clear, I’m not a cheerleader for that story. You know, you don’t write a book called The Bitter Struggle if you’re a cheerleader. But I think that story is largely undiminished by these events here. Warzel: What about China? Where are they better off? Are they worse off than they were? Buchanan: They’re worse off. They’re absolutely worse off. Because there was a bipartisan consensus that was forming on denying China access to computing power. But they had big allies that were saying, You know, let’s sell China the chips . And those allies were having some success. Chief amongst some, Jensen. David Sacks, Trump’s—my successor, as you know—AI adviser to the president, was advocating for this, at least based on the reporting. President Trump had advocated for in some context. And now the bipartisan consensus has, at least so far, started to harden against them. That is bad for China’s access to compute, and ultimately that is bad for China. Warzel: Ben Buchanan: Thank you for coming and helping to demystify this; talking about it in these very plain terms. I wanna have you back on, to talk about the regulation part of this, later. But this has been very helpful. Buchanan: It is great to talk about this subject, and it’s great to have interest in this subject of the chips and chip controls. Because this is a wonky subject for sure—that now has gotten this gloss of a sex scandal and a spy story. But I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say this is one of the most important subjects in the world for U.S. national policy. Warzel: And we’ll keep following it. Thank you very much, Ben, for coming on. Buchanan: Thanks for having me. [ Music ] Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. This episode of Galaxy Brain was produced by Hadley Robinson, with story editing by Dave Shaw; the video was edited by Alisa Selman; and the audio was engineered by Rob Smierciak. items.title: Petrol price reduced by Re1 per litre; diesel increased by Rs2 per litre
items.description: The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Re1 per litre while raising that of diesel by Rs2 per litre, after snapping a 12-day streak of consecutive reductions in the rate of petrol the previous day. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs322 per litre and HSD at Rs357 on Nov 21 (Saturday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Following Tuesday’s reduction of the petrol price to Rs325 per litre, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar highlighted the government’s “proactive measures including policy changes and structural reforms in petroleum policy” that had brought prices back down from their April 3 peak and provided relief through a fuel subsidy scheme. “The government of Pakistan remains committed to continue making all possible efforts to ease the financial burden on the common man amid global challenges,” he said. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation. The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

items.title: Présidentielle en France : Mediapart met un coup de projecteur sur les liens entre Teddy Riner et le roi du Maroc
items.description: Teddy Riner va-t-il payer cher sa photo , torse nu et drape du drapeau francais, en une de l'hebdomadaire Paris-Match ? Dans un article paru le 19 novembre, Mediapart souligne que le cliche – qui fait couler beaucoup d'encre ces derniers jours – a ete pris au Maroc. Un element de la legende « hautement symbolique », a raille le media en ligne, qui s'est attarde sur les liens entre le triple champion olympique francais et le roi du Maroc, Mohammed VI. Selon cette source, Teddy Riner serait en effet le principal actionnaire – a hauteur de 50 % – d'une societe de transport en voiture de luxe, Pullman Limousine, qui exploite une partie du parc automobile d'une societe cette fois-ci integralement detenue par l'athlete : Pullman Rent. Deterrant une note d'une commissaire aux comptes, datant de septembre 2023, Mediapart rapporte ainsi que « la clientele de Pullman Limousine Services » est « composee a 90 % par la delegation du roi du Maroc ». Une societe qui, selon la meme source, a realise entre 2019 et 2022 la bagatelle de 8,7 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires et reverse 1,6 million d'euros a Pullman Rent. Des sommes en grande partie concentrees sur la seule annee 2022, a hauteur de 7,1 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires, ou le souverain du royaume cherifien a sejourne pres de quatre mois en France. Redresse pour « avantages occultes » Une activite professionnelle qui a par ailleurs valu a Teddy Riner des deboires avec le Fisc, ce dernier accusant le judoka d'etre le « conducteur exclusif » de deux vehicules de sa societe de location, vehicules dont les charges imputees a sa societe « ont constitue des remunerations et avantages occultes pour Teddy Riner » a hauteur de 289 000 euros. Ainsi dans le collimateur de la DGFiP depuis 2019, au titre des exercices 2016 et 2017, l'athlete et entrepreneur a perdu mi-octobre en justice devant la cour administrative d'appel de Versailles qui a conforte l'administration fiscale et souligne une « intention deliberee » de « minorer l'impot ». Par ailleurs, le fraîchement declare candidat a la presidentielle est egalement poursuivi sur ses activites immobilieres , le Fisc lui reclamant pres de 245 000 euros.

items.title: Sénégal-Maroc U23 : Vieira et Dia appelés à unir leurs forces pour viser la CAN et les JO
items.description: La double confrontation entre le Sénégal et le Maroc, prévue les 22 et 30 mars 2027, dépasse le simple enjeu d'une qualification à la CAN U23 et aux JO de Los Angeles 2028. Entre le contentieux de la dernière CAN senior, les ambitions olympiques et la rivalité sportive entre les deux pays, les Lionceaux joueront bien plus qu'une place en phase finale. Pour franchir cet obstacle, Serigne Saliou Dia devra pouvoir compter sur toutes les forces disponibles. Patrick Vieira est notamment attendu pour faciliter la mise à disposition des jeunes internationaux de l'équipe A éligibles aux U23. Des triomphes sénégalaises en terre marocaine Les Sénégalais ont obtenu leur billet pour le dernier tour en éliminant le Soudan du Sud (0-0 à Juba, 3-1 au retour). Une qualification qui n'a toutefois pas totalement dissipé les interrogations sur le rendement du groupe. Face au Maroc, champion d'Afrique U23 en titre et détenteur du titre mondial chez les U20, le défi sera d'une autre dimension. La CAN U23 prévue en Égypte constitue également le passage obligé vers les Jeux olympiques de Los Angeles 2028, où l'Afrique ambitionne de placer deux représentants. Les finalistes devraient ainsi décrocher les précieux billets olympiques. Mais cette affiche porte aussi le poids d'une histoire récente. Le 18 janvier 2026, à Rabat, le Sénégal avait battu le Maroc (1-0) après prolongation en finale de la CAN senior, grâce à Pape Gueye. Une victoire sur le terrain que le jury d'appel de la CAF a ensuite transformée en succès marocain sur tapis vert, en attribuant un forfait de 3-0 aux Lions. La Fédération sénégalaise de football a saisi le Tribunal arbitral du sport pour contester cette décision. Après l'audience du 8 octobre, le verdict est attendu à la fin du mois de novembre. Les retrouvailles de mars auront donc une saveur particulière. Entre le Maroc et le Sénégal, les retrouvailles n’ont plus rien d’anodin depuis la dernière CAN. Mais s’il est un terrain où les Sénégalais ont de quoi nourrir leur confiance, c’est bien celui du royaume. En juin 2026, les Lionceaux y ont décroché à Rabat leur deuxième titre de champion d’Afrique U17. Quelques mois plus tôt, les Lions avaient eux aussi dominé les Marocains en finale de la CAN senior, une victoire acquise sur la pelouse, même si le TAS doit encore se prononcer sur l’issue de cette rencontre. Le beach soccer vient compléter ce tableau : avec huit couronnes continentales en treize éditions, dont deux conquises sur le sol marocain, en 2011 et 2013, le Sénégal y règne en maître. Autant de preuves que les sélections sénégalaises savent briller chez leur rival. Vieira et Dia, une même ambition Pour éviter de laisser passer cette double opportunité, Serigne Saliou Dia aura besoin d'un groupe étoffé. Le sélectionneur pourrait notamment bénéficier de l'apport de plusieurs jeunes internationaux de l'équipe A. Mamadou Sarr, Mamadou Diakhon, Ibrahima Mbaye, Paul Mendy ou encore le gardien Mamour Ndiaye représentent des profils susceptibles d'apporter de l'expérience et de la qualité aux Lionceaux, sous réserve de leur éligibilité et de leur disponibilité en club. Patrick Vieira aura donc un rôle important à jouer dans cette articulation. La qualification de l'équipe A à la CAN 2027 permet d'envisager une meilleure coordination entre les deux staffs. L'objectif n'est pas de déshabiller une sélection pour renforcer l'autre, mais de construire une stratégie commune autour d'une échéance qui engage l'avenir du football sénégalais en mars 2027. Le Maroc suit déjà cette logique. Selon la presse marocaine, Mohamed Ouahbi est également appelé à faciliter la mise à disposition de plusieurs jeunes talents de l'équipe A au profit de la sélection olympique. Ali Maamar, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Yassir Zabiri, Yassine Gessime et Samir El Mourabit figurent parmi les joueurs évoqués. Abdellah Ouazane, Soufian El Faouzi et Abdelhamid Aït Boudlal constituent d'autres profils susceptibles d'enrichir ce vivier. Le Maroc entend ainsi mobiliser sa jeune génération pour défendre son statut continental et retrouver les Jeux. Ne pas répéter les erreurs de 2023 Le Sénégal connaît pourtant le prix d'une mauvaise coordination entre ses sélections. En mars 2023, les Lionceaux avaient dominé le Mali (3-1) à Diamniadio avant de s'effondrer au retour à Bamako (0-3). Cette élimination les avait privés de la CAN U23 et des Jeux olympiques de Paris 2024. Dion Lopy et Formose Mendy, initialement concernés par le groupe de Demba Mbaye, avaient entre-temps rejoint l'équipe A après leur convocation incomprehensible par Aliou Cissé. Ce précédent doit servir de leçon. Quatre ans plus tard, le Sénégal retrouve une situation où la gestion des effectifs peut peser aussi lourd que les choix tactiques. Le Maroc anticipe déjà la mobilisation de ses jeunes internationaux. La Tanière ne peut se permettre de laisser passer cette opportunité. En mars, les deux sélections auront 180 minutes voire plus pour se départager. Au-delà de la rivalité et du contentieux qui opposent les deux fédérations, les Lionceaux devront surtout répondre présents sur le terrain. Pour atteindre l'Égypte et rêver de Los Angeles, Vieira et Dia devront parler le même langage. Cette fois, l'union des forces ne doit pas rester un slogan : elle doit devenir une stratégie. Par Cheikh Gora DIOP

items.title: La présidentielle française de 2027 pourrait affaiblir le soutien européen à l’Ukraine et provoquer des divisions au sein de l’UE
items.description: L'election presidentielle francaise de 2027 pourrait entraîner une revision de la politique de Paris envers l'Ukraine et compliquer la poursuite du soutien europeen a Kiev. Dans une enquete publiee le 20 novembre, Politico rapporte les preoccupations de plusieurs responsables europeens et ukrainiens face a la possibilite d'un changement de cap a l'elysee. Le premier tour est prevu le 18 avril 2027 et le second, si necessaire, le 2 mai. Selon les sondages cites dans l'enquete, Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Melenchon figurent parmi les candidats susceptibles d'acceder au second tour. Tous deux contestent certains choix d'Emmanuel Macron concernant le conflit ukrainien. Marine Le Pen estime que les difficultes budgetaires francaises ne permettent plus de maintenir l'aide financiere a Kiev. Elle souhaite mettre fin a l'assistance, tout en conservant certaines cooperations militaires, notamment la formation des soldats ukrainiens. Jean-Luc Melenchon s'oppose, quant a lui, aux frappes ukrainiennes en profondeur sur le territoire russe. Il avait aussi evoque un referendum dans le Donbass permettant a ses habitants de se prononcer sur leur avenir. La proposition, critiquee a Kiev, avait ensuite fait l'objet de precisions de sa part. Le soutien europeen et les sanctions contre Moscou en question Pour les responsables interroges, les consequences d'une alternance francaise depasseraient la question du financement de Kiev. Leur principale preoccupation concerne la capacite de l'Union europeenne a maintenir une position commune. La France joue un role important dans la coordination. Elle copreside la « Coalition des volontaires », participe aux discussions sur les garanties de securite et contribue aux positions europeennes sur les negociations de paix. « En matiere de soutien financier, la France n'a jamais figure parmi les dix premiers. Mais concernant le risque de rupture du consensus europeen, ce serait un veritable defi », a declare un responsable ukrainien a Politico. Les avis restent toutefois partages. Sur les huit responsables et diplomates europeens et ukrainiens interroges, environ la moitie redoutent un affaiblissement du soutien a Kiev. Les autres estiment que les candidats pourraient moderer leurs positions une fois au pouvoir. Un eventuel changement a l'elysee pourrait aussi peser sur les sanctions contre Moscou. Selon un diplomate occidental cite par le media, le Rassemblement national chercherait a les assouplir. Leur renouvellement exigeant l'unanimite des etats membres, un veto francais risquerait d'empecher leur prolongation. a ses yeux, la hausse des prix de l'energie raviverait l'interet de certains pays europeens pour le petrole et le gaz russes. Berlin veut preserver le financement de Kiev La perspective d'un changement de politique francaise conduit Berlin a rechercher des mecanismes de financement moins exposes aux blocages. Selon le media, le chancelier allemand, Friedrich Merz, souhaite inscrire l'aide a Kiev dans le prochain budget europeen et permettre que certaines decisions soient prises a la majorite qualifiee plutot qu'a l'unanimite. De son cote, Volodymyr Zelensky tente de relativiser les consequences d'une eventuelle alternance francaise. « Nous travaillerons avec celui ou celle que les Francais eliront », a-t-il declare a Politico. Moscou, pour sa part, considere que la poursuite de l'aide militaire occidentale a l'Ukraine contribue uniquement a prolonger le conflit, une position souvent rappelee par les autorites russes.

items.title: Deepfake : des vidéos de plus en plus difficiles à démasquer
items.description: Des videos truquees mettant en scene des personnalites publiques circulent de plus en plus sur les reseaux sociaux. Elles sont parfois si realistes qu'il devient difficile de distinguer le vrai du faux. Des sequences mettant en scene des joueurs de football, des personnalites publiques ou d'autres personnes connues circulent regulierement sur les reseaux sociaux. Certaines sont tellement convaincantes qu'il devient difficile de soupconner une manipulation. Ces contenus, appeles deepfakes , sont realises a l'aide de technologies d'intelligence artificielle capables de modifier ou de generer des images et des voix. Des outils d'IA rendent les manipulations plus realistes Des outils comme Veo, DeepSwap ou FaceFusion facilitent la creation de videos truquees. Ils permettent notamment de generer des sequences, de remplacer un visage ou de reproduire certains mouvements et expressions. Avec les progres de ces technologies, les anomalies autrefois relativement faciles a reperer deviennent moins evidentes. Un decalage entre les mouvements des levres et la voix, des gestes incoherents ou des mouvements de mains peu naturels pouvaient autrefois eveiller les soupcons. Aujourd'hui, ces indices ne suffisent plus toujours a identifier une video manipulee. La qualite visuelle d'une sequence ne constitue donc plus une garantie d'authenticite. Une video nette, avec des mouvements fluides et des expressions naturelles, peut-elle aussi avoir ete generee ou modifiee par l'intelligence artificielle. Des outils de detection utiles, mais pas infaillibles Pour analyser une video suspecte, certains outils en ligne peuvent apporter une premiere indication. C'est notamment le cas de Hive Moderation et de Deepware Scanner, qui proposent des analyses destinees a reperer d'eventuelles manipulations. Cependant, leurs resultats doivent etre interpretes avec prudence. Ces outils peuvent passer a cote de certaines videos truquees ou signaler a tort un contenu authentique. Aucun resultat ne suffit donc, a lui seul, a confirmer qu'une video est vraie ou fausse. Cinq reflexes a adopter face a une video suspecte En l'absence de certitude, la verification de la source reste essentielle. Avant de partager une video, plusieurs reflexes peuvent aider a eviter les pieges. Rechercher l'origine de la video, verifier le contexte, rechercher d'autres sources, analyser les images et le son, utiliser les outils de detection avec prudence. Face a la sophistication croissante des deepfakes, la vigilance reste indispensable. Une video peut sembler parfaitement reelle sans l'etre. Avant de croire ou de partager, il faut toujours verifier.
